media.title: Travel Explorer

tool_config.idea: Explore earlier ways of travelling one at a time and sort them into long ago and about a hundred years ago, so the travel story of the chapter is clear before the number lessons begin. The tour ends with an open question about how many vehicles there are in a state, which hands over to big numbers.
tool_config.title: Travel Explorer
tool_config.screen: A warm storybook village by a wide river, drawn as a polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation: a dirt road with a bullock cart under trees, a wooden boat and a sailing ship on the river, a footpath, and an old train on a track at the edge of the village. One scene only, no crowd. A row of seven large mode cards runs along the bottom: On foot, Animals, Boat, Sailing ship, Bullock cart, Train and Car. Only one card is active at a time. Tapping a card plays a short use animation in the middle of the scene (a walker crossing the village, animals pulling and carrying, the boat drifting over the river, the ship sailing, the bullock cart rolling, the train moving along the track, a car on the road) and shows one short sentence from the chapter's opening story in a large caption box. When Animals is active, three large chips appear: Animals used for travelling (bullocks, horses, donkeys, mules, elephants), Hilly and snow-covered regions (yaks, dogs, reindeer) and Deserts (camels). A time strip across the top has two labelled bays, Thousands of years ago and About a hundred years ago, and the student drags a mode card into a bay. A counter shows how many of the 7 cards are sorted. Fixed controls: Back and Next in the same places on every card, a Replay button for the animation, a Hint button, a Restart button and progress dots.
feedback: Tapping a mode card lights it up, plays its short animation and shows one sentence from the story. Only one card is active at a time.

A card dropped in the right bay locks in with a soft chime and a tick. A card dropped in the wrong bay slides back and shows the story's sentence that places it, for example: About a hundred years ago there were animal-drawn carts, cars and trains.
The counter shows at once how many of the 7 cards are sorted.
The two open questions at the end are never marked wrong: the screen says Your answer may differ and shows Next.
tool_config.done_when: All 7 cards are sorted, the two open questions have been answered once, and the student has pressed Next at the end of the tour.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1: tap On foot and watch the walker. How did people travel long distances thousands of years ago when they had no animal and no boat? Answer: on foot.

Card 2: open Animals and tap each group. Which animals does the story name for hilly and snow-covered regions, and which for deserts? Answer: yaks, dogs and reindeer in hilly and snow-covered regions, and camels in deserts.
Card 3: tap Boat and Bullock cart. Which was invented first? Answer: the boat, because boats were probably the first form of transport humans invented, much before bullock carts.

Card 4: drag each of the 7 cards into a bay. Answer: Thousands of years ago holds On foot, Animals, Boat and Sailing ship (4 cards). About a hundred years ago holds Bullock cart, Train and Car (3 cards).
Card 5: read the counter. How many ways of travelling are sorted in all? Answer: 4 + 3 = 7.

media.instructions_for_student: The student sees how people travelled long ago and about a hundred years ago, and that boats came much before bullock carts.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Travel Explorer
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S1.T1.C2.2D1
- Tool type: Exploration
- Textbook source: We the Travellers - I, the opening page and the passage "Travelling, Now and Then": boats as the first transport, animals for hills, snow and deserts, the vehicles of about a hundred years ago, the trip questions and the question about the vehicles in a state. No number is calculated (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees how people travelled long ago and about a hundred years ago, and that boats came much before bullock carts.
- Out of scope: reading or writing large numbers, distances, speeds, and counting vehicles. The question about vehicles in a state is only a guess here.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- The stage shows a flat storybook illustration of a riverside village, with no crowds: a footpath and a dirt road with two trees on the left, a wide river across the middle with a small wooden boat and a sailing ship on it, and a railway line on the right edge with an old steam train.
- Two big picture panels cover the middle of the scene, side by side: a sand desert on the left and a snow-covered hill on the right. Under them lies a tray of 4 animal cut-outs: camel, yak, dog, reindeer.
- Instruction line: "Which place suits which animal? Drag each animal to its place."
- The child is invited to touch the camel first.
2. Scene and Objects
- Animal cut-outs are flat drawings, each about 12% of the stage width, with the name written under each. Each landscape panel has its name on top: "Desert" and "Snow-covered hills". A panel holds up to 4 animals.
- After Activity 2 the panels disappear. A time strip appears across the top of the stage with two bays: "Thousands of years ago" on the left and "About a hundred years ago" on the right. Each bay is about 45% of the stage width.
- Along the bottom of the stage lie 7 travel cards, each about 12% of the stage width: "On foot" (a flat drawn walker with a bundle), "Animals" (a flat drawn bullock and a camel), "Boat" (photo cut-out of a wooden boat), "Sailing ship" (photo cut-out), "Bullock cart" (photo cut-out), "Train" (photo cut-out of an old steam train) and "Car" (photo cut-out of an old car). Only one card is active at a time.
- Goal chips on the stage: "Animals placed: 0 of 4" in Activity 1, "First and later" in Activity 2, "Sorted: 0 of 7" in Activity 3.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a card or an animal and drop it on a panel, a slot or a bay. Tap a card to light it and play its short animation in the middle of the scene: a walker crossing the village, animals pulling and carrying, the boat drifting, the ship sailing, the bullock cart rolling, the train moving along the track, a car on the road. A caption under the scene shows one sentence from the story.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" and one big "Check" button that becomes "Next" when the activity is done. Dragging a card out of a bay takes it back. Reset returns the activity to its start.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Which place suits which animal? Drag each animal to its place." Goal chip: "Animals placed: 0 of 4". The child drags camel, yak, dog and reindeer onto the two panels, then presses Check. Guess: the child places all 4 animals before anything is marked. Result: the camel stays in "Desert" and the yak, dog and reindeer stay in "Snow-covered hills"; each wakes up and walks on its panel. Why line: "Yaks, dogs and reindeer travelled in hilly and snow-covered regions. Camels travelled in deserts." Help: guided, each animal has its name label and each panel has its name.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Which came first, the boat or the bullock cart? Drag them into order." Goal chip: "First and later". Two cards, "Boat" and "Bullock cart", sit in a tray. Two slots appear: "First" and "Later". Guess: the child places both cards, then presses Check. Result: the Boat card goes to "First" with a tick and the river scene glows. Why line: "Boats were probably the first transport people invented, much before bullock carts." Help: guided, both cards show a small picture and the river scene stays visible.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Sort all 7 travel cards by time. Drag each card into a bay." Goal chip: "Sorted: 0 of 7". Start: 7 cards, both bays empty, the chip counts the cards placed. Guess: the child drops every card where they think it belongs before pressing Check; nothing is marked earlier. Result: "On foot", "Animals", "Boat" and "Sailing ship" lock into "Thousands of years ago"; "Bullock cart", "Train" and "Car" lock into "About a hundred years ago"; each locked card shows a green tick. Why line: "4 + 3 = 7: four ways of travelling are from thousands of years ago and three from about a hundred years ago." Help: independent, only the card names show.
- Star Challenge 1 (open). Goal line: "When was the last time you went on a long trip? Where did you go? How did you travel? What was the duration of your trip? How much distance did you cover? Ask the elders who went with you to help you answer these questions." Goal chip: "My trip". The child taps the travel card for how they travelled, then one chip for how long ("Less than an hour", "A few hours", "A day or more") and one chip for how far ("2-digit km", "3-digit km", "4-digit km or more"). Guess: the chips are the child's own guess. Result: no right or wrong. Line: "Your answer is your own. Your answer may differ." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (open). Goal line: "Do you know how many vehicles are currently there in your state?" Goal chip: "My guess". Three chips: "4 digits", "5 digits", "More than 5 digits". Guess: the child taps one chip. Result: the chip glows; a small line: "Big numbers help us count vehicles. Next stop: how do we write a number as big as ten thousand?" Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- By placing animals and cards in time order the child sees that travel has a long history: first feet and animals, then boats and ships, then carts, cars and trains, and that the number of vehicles grew. The child says: "Journeys use big numbers: how far, how long and how many vehicles." No arithmetic rule is taught here.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: a placed card gets a green tick and a soft chime, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the strip says "Yes, that is right!" and Next unlocks.
- Mistake: an animal in the wrong panel (Activity 1) -> red strip, small shake, "Look at the ground: sand or snow? Which animal suits it?" The wrong animal slides back to the tray and both panel names pulse.
- Mistake: Boat put in "Later" (Activity 2) -> "Think about the river. People built boats a very long time ago."
- Mistake: "Train" or "Car" dropped in "Thousands of years ago" (Activity 3) -> "Trains and cars were on the road only about a hundred years ago." The card slides back.
- Mistake: "Bullock cart" dropped in "Thousands of years ago" -> "The story names animal-drawn carts for about a hundred years ago." The bay label pulses.
- Mistake: "Boat", "Sailing ship", "On foot" or "Animals" dropped in "About a hundred years ago" -> "People walked, rode animals and built boats and ships long before that." The bay label pulses.
- Hints: (1) "Look at each picture. Which one needs a road, a rail or an engine?" (2) The two bays glow and the cards that are not placed wiggle. (3) The tool shows the answer for one card: "Boat belongs to Thousands of years ago" and puts it there.
- Edge cases: Check with a card still in the tray -> "Place every card first." The tray pulses. The open stars are never marked wrong.
7. Ending
- Star Challenge 1 is done when the child taps a travel card and the two chips once. Star Challenge 2 is done when the child taps one chip.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "People first travelled on foot and on animals." "Boats were probably the first transport people invented, much before bullock carts." "About a hundred years ago there were far fewer vehicles than there are now." Think and talk: "How many vehicles do you think there are in your state: 4 digits, 5 digits or more? Why?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: riverside village illustration with footpath, road, river and railway; desert panel; snow-covered hill panel; flat drawings of camel, yak, dog, reindeer, walker with a bundle, bullock and camel pair; photo cut-outs of a wooden boat, a sailing ship, a bullock cart, an old steam train and an old car; time strip with two bays. English only, short sentences.

topics.summary: A journey is full of numbers: how far we go, how long it takes and how many vehicles are on the road. People once travelled on foot, on animals and in boats. Today there are many more vehicles, and big numbers help us count them.

content.text:
When was the last time you went on a long trip? Where did you go? How did you travel? What was the duration of your trip? How much distance did you cover? Ask the elders who went with you to help you answer these questions.
Human beings have always been interested in travelling. About a hundred years ago, there were far fewer vehicles than today. There were animal-drawn carts, cars, and trains. Long before this, thousands of years ago, people travelled long distances on foot or used animals to travel from one place to another. They also built boats and ships to travel across lakes, rivers, and seas. Boats were probably the first form of transport invented by humans, much before bullock carts! Do you know how many vehicles are currently there in your state?

media.composition: One row of 7 picture cards in time order with a bracket and a count over each group, a time arrow under the row and the sum at the bottom.
media.description: Seven picture cards show ways of travelling in a row. A blue bracket labelled "Long ago" spans four cards: a person walking labelled "on foot", a horse rider labelled "on animals", a wooden boat labelled "in boats", and a sailing ship labelled "in ships". An amber bracket labelled "About a hundred years ago" spans three cards: an ox cart labelled "animal-drawn carts", a car labelled "cars", and a train labelled "trains". The boat and cart cards have thick purple borders. Under the groups sit a blue "4" and an amber "3". A grey arrow points from "Older" to "Newer" above "4 + 3 = 7".
media.source_figure: A then and now line: a boat, a bullock cart, a train, a car and a bicycle in a row from long ago to today, no dates and no numbers.
media.teaching_notes: Ask which came first, a boat or a bullock cart, and let students point at the two purple-outlined cards. The arrow shows older to newer only; it does not say how many years separate the cards. Do not add speeds or dates.

They built boats and ships to cross lakes, rivers and seas. Boats were probably the first form of transport humans invented, much before bullock carts. Check: foot, animals, boats, ships, carts, cars, trains make 7 names. Answer: 7 ways of travelling are named, and a boat is older than a bullock cart

content.text: Human beings have always been interested in travelling. About a hundred years ago, there were far fewer vehicles than today. There were animal-drawn carts, cars, and trains. Long before this, thousands of years ago, people travelled long distances on foot or used animals to travel from one place to another. They also built boats and ships to travel across lakes, rivers, and seas. Boats were probably the first form of transport invented by humans, much before bullock carts!

Worked example: The opening story names ways of travelling. Long ago: on foot, on animals, in boats and in ships. About a hundred years ago: animal-drawn carts, cars and trains. How many ways of travelling does the story name in all, and which is older, a boat or a bullock cart?
1. Long ago the story names 4 ways: on foot, on animals, in boats and in ships.
2. About a hundred years ago it names 3 vehicles: animal-drawn carts, cars and trains.
3. Add the two groups: 4 + 3 = 7.
4. The story says boats were probably the first transport humans invented, much before bullock carts.
5. So a boat is older than a bullock cart.
6. Check: foot, animals, boats, ships, carts, cars, trains make 7 names.
Answer: 7 ways of travelling are named, and a boat is older than a bullock cart

content.text:
How do you write numbers to show several thousand objects?
Let us start with 1,000. What numbers do we get when we keep adding a thousand?
What number do we get when we add a thousand to 9,000? We get ten thousand. How do we write this number?

1. Predict first: you keep adding one thousand, 1,000, 2,000, 3,000 and so on. Which number comes after 9,000?
2. Each step adds one more thousand. After 9 thousands, one more thousand makes 10 thousands.
3. 9,000 + 1,000 = 10,000. We say ten thousand.
4. Rule: 10 thousands make 1 ten thousand, and a number with 10 thousands needs a new place.

4. 10 thousands make 1 ten thousand, so write 1 in the new TTh column: 10,150.
5. Say it: ten thousand one hundred fifty.
6. Check: 10,150 − 9,150 = 1,000.

content.text:
Look at the table below and notice the pattern of writing numbers. In the place value chart, we have added another column, TTh. It stands for ten thousand.
10 Ones = 1 Ten = 10
10 Tens = 1 Hundred = 100
10 Hundreds = 1 Thousand = 1,000
In the same way, 10 Thousands = Ten Thousand = 10,000.
We use a comma to help us read large numbers easily.
Do you remember how we read and write numbers in the Indian place value system? We use the same ten digits 0 to 9 in different places to write larger numbers.
For example, 1,380 = 1 Thousand + 3 Hundreds + 8 Tens + 0 Ones.
9,123 = 9 Thousands + 1 Hundred + 2 Tens + 3 Ones.

content.text:
Worked example: Put the digits of 52,525 in the place value chart and say what each digit is worth.
1. Write the digits from the left: TTh 5, Th 2, H 5, T 2, O 5.
2. The 5 in TTh is 5 ten thousands: 5 × 10,000 = 50,000.
3. The 2 in Th is 2 thousands: 2 × 1,000 = 2,000.
4. The 5 in H is 5 hundreds: 5 × 100 = 500.
5. The 2 in T is 2 tens: 2 × 10 = 20.
6. The 5 in O is 5 ones: 5 × 1 = 5.
7. Check: 50,000 + 2,000 + 500 + 20 + 5 = 52,525.
Answer: The three 5s are worth 50,000, 500 and 5, and the number is 52,525

content.text:
1. The first box is $1,000$ and each box adds $1,000$ more.
2. Fill the empty boxes: $3,000$, $4,000$, $5,000$, $6,000$, $7,000$ and $8,000$.
3. Check the last box: $8,000 + 1,000 = 9,000$.
4. Add one more thousand: $9,000 + 1,000 = 10,000$.
5. $10$ thousands make $1$ ten thousand, so we say ten thousand.
[Image: Reading and writing large numbers: Ans1: solution]
6. Write $1$ in the new ten thousands column and $0$ in thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, with the comma before the last three digits: $10,000$.
Answer: The boxes are $1,000$ to $9,000$, and $9,000 + 1,000 = 10,000$, which is ten thousand
[Image: Reading and writing large numbers: Ans1: solution (continued)]

tool_config.idea: Read numbers beyond ten thousand by matching the numeral, the number name and the place value tokens: say the part before the comma and add thousand, then the hundreds, tens and ones, and skip every place that holds 0.
tool_config.title: Number Reading Challenge
tool_config.screen: A large, readable railway station destination board in a warm 3D station scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The board shows ONE numeral at a time in very large type with its comma; it is the largest thing on screen. Under the board sit three clear panels: a place value chart with the columns TTh, Th, H, T and O, a tray of place value token pictures in the book's colours (10,000 purple, 1,000 green, 100 orange, 10 blue, 1 pink), and a number name strip with empty slots. Below them is a tray of number name word cards (for example Ten, Thirteen, Forty-five, thousand, hundred, one, twenty, twenty-four, five, sixty-seven). Controls: drag a word card into a slot of the name strip, tap a slot to take its card out, a Check button, a Show tokens button that fills the chart and the token tray for the numeral, a Hear it button that says the name aloud, Back and Next in the same places on every card, a Hint button, a Reset button and progress dots. Read-outs: the chart digits light up one column at a time as the matching words are placed, and a counter shows the card number out of 7.
feedback: A word card dropped in the right slot snaps in and lights the matching column of the chart and the matching tokens. A card in a wrong slot springs back and the column that it should name blinks.
A place that holds 0 stays dark and a small note says there is no word for a zero place.
When the name is complete the board reads it aloud with a short pause at the comma.
A name that is not right points to the part before the comma as the first thing to check, and never shows the full name.
tool_config.done_when: All 7 cards are matched with their numeral, name and tokens, and the last two cards are built correctly without a hint.

media.instructions_for_student: The student reads a five-digit number by saying the part before the comma with thousand, then the hundreds, tens and ones, and skipping every place that holds 0.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Number Reading Challenge
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S5.T5.C12.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: We the Travellers - I, Reading and writing large numbers: the token table (10,033 to 45,867) and Let Us Do Question 2, number to name (7,209 to 81,200) (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student reads a five-digit number by saying the part before the comma with "thousand", then the hundreds, tens and ones, and skips every place that holds 0.
- Out of scope: writing a number from its name, comparing numbers, numbers beyond 5 digits, other number systems.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A railway station departure board on a dark wall fills the top 35% of the stage and shows ONE number in big glowing dot-matrix digits with its comma: 21,436. A small speaker icon sits in its corner.
- Under the board is a place value chart with five columns TTh, Th, H, T, O. Token pictures sit in the columns: 2 purple 10,000 tokens, 1 green 1,000 token, 4 orange 100 tokens, 3 blue 10 tokens, 6 pink 1 tokens. Under the chart is a name strip with 6 empty word slots and a tray of 8 cream word cards.
- Instruction line: "Look at the number. Tap the part you say first." The child is invited to touch the digits on the board.
2. Scene and Objects
- Tokens are rounded rectangles with their value written on them. The strip always has 6 slots, so the slot count gives no clue. In the token challenges a tray of digit tiles 0 to 9 replaces the word cards; tiles stay in the tray when used.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a word card into the leftmost free slot, or tap a card to send it there. Tap a placed card to send it back. Drag digit tiles into the chart columns, one tile per column; tapping a column clears it.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" and one big "Check" button that becomes "Next" when the pill is done. When a name is right the board reads it aloud with a short pause at the comma; the speaker icon mutes the voice.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Look at the number. Tap the part you say first." Goal chip: "Read it". Number 21,436 with tokens: 20,000 + 1,000 + 400 + 30 + 6 = 21,436. Guess: the child taps the digits they say first; the answer is 21, the part before the comma. Then the child builds the name from the tray "twenty-one", "thousand", "four", "hundred", "thirty-six", "twelve", "forty", "sixty-three". Result: the board reads "Twenty-one thousand four hundred thirty-six" and the chart columns light one by one. Why: "21 before the comma is twenty-one thousand, then 436 is four hundred thirty-six." Help: guided, tokens and chart shown, a comma arrow marks where the thousands part ends.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Read the number. Two digits can make one word." Goal chip: "Read it". Number 16,418 with tokens: 10,000 + 6,000 + 400 + 10 + 8 = 16,418. Guess: the child taps "eighteen" or "eighty" for the digits 1 and 8 of the Tens and Ones columns. Tray: "sixteen", "thousand", "four", "hundred", "eighteen", "sixty", "forty", "eighty". Result: "Sixteen thousand four hundred eighteen". Why: "1 Ten and 8 Ones make 18, said eighteen, and 16 before the comma is sixteen thousand." Help: guided, tokens and chart shown.
- Activity 3 (guided). Goal line: "Some places hold 0. Do we say them?" Goal chip: "Read it". Number 17,060, tokens only in TTh, Th and T: 10,000 + 7,000 + 60 = 17,060; the H and O columns are empty. Guess: before building, the child taps the columns that will not be said (H and O); they turn grey with the tag "skip". Tray: "seventeen", "thousand", "sixty", "hundred", "six", "seventy", "zero". Result: "Seventeen thousand sixty". Why: "The Hundreds and Ones places hold 0, so we skip them: seventeen thousand sixty." Help: guided, empty columns are marked.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Read this number. Build its name." Goal chip: "Read it". Number 70,800, no tokens, chart digits only: 7, 0, 8, 0, 0. Guess: the child taps how many words the name has: "3 words", "4 words" or "5 words" (the answer is 4). Tray: "seventy", "thousand", "eight", "hundred", "eighty", "seven", "zero". Result: "Seventy thousand eight hundred". Why: "70 before the comma is seventy thousand, H 8 is eight hundred, and the Tens and Ones hold 0, so nothing more is said." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "Fill in the token table. Write the number and write its digits in the ten thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens and ones columns." Goal chip: "Rows done: 0 of 2". Row 1: tokens one 10,000, three 10s and three 1s, name "Ten thousand thirty-three" given. Row 2: number 10,458 and name "Ten thousand four hundred fifty-eight" given. Guess: before each row the child taps how many digits the number has ("4", "5" or "6"). The child drags digit tiles into the chart: row 1 gets 1, 0, 0, 3, 3 and the board prints 10,033; row 2 gets 1, 0, 4, 5, 8. Why: "10,000 + 30 + 3 = 10,033" and "10,000 + 400 + 50 + 8 = 10,458". Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "Fill in the token table." Goal chip: "Rows done: 0 of 4". Row (a): tokens one 10,000, one 1,000, two 100s, one 10 and four 1s, chart digits 1, 1, 2, 1, 4 given; the child writes the number by dragging tiles into a 5 slot Number box with a comma gap, and builds the name from the tray "eleven", "thousand", "two", "hundred", "fourteen", "twelve", "twenty", "forty". Row (b): 13,520 and "Thirteen thousand five hundred twenty" given; digits 1, 3, 5, 2, 0. Row (c): 20,000 and "Twenty thousand" given; digits 2, 0, 0, 0, 0. Row (d): 45,867 and "Forty-five thousand eight hundred sixty-seven" given; digits 4, 5, 8, 6, 7. Guess: before each row the child taps how many places will hold 0 ("0", "1", "2", "3" or "4"). Result for (a): 11,214 and "Eleven thousand two hundred fourteen". Why: "10,000 + 1,000 + 200 + 10 + 4 = 11,214" and, for (c), "Two 10,000 tokens make 20,000, so the other four places hold 0." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "Fill in the blanks appropriately. Use commas as required. Write the number name of each of these numbers." Goal chip: "Names: 0 of 4". Numbers, one at a time: 7,209; 10,599; 13,579; 45,045. Trays: 7,209: "seven", "thousand", "two", "hundred", "nine", "seventy", "twenty", "zero". 10,599: "ten", "thousand", "five", "hundred", "ninety-nine", "fifteen", "fifty-nine", "ninety". 13,579: "thirteen", "thousand", "five", "hundred", "seventy-nine", "thirty", "seventy", "ninety-seven". 45,045: two "forty-five" cards, "thousand", "hundred", "four", "fifty-four". Guess: before building, the child taps the columns that will not be said. Results: "Seven thousand two hundred nine", "Ten thousand five hundred ninety-nine", "Thirteen thousand five hundred seventy-nine", "Forty-five thousand forty-five". Why for 45,045: "The Hundreds place holds 0, so we skip it: forty-five thousand forty-five." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4. Same goal line. Goal chip: "Names: 0 of 4". Numbers: 39,593; 50,005; 26,050; 81,200. Trays: 39,593: "thirty-nine", "thousand", "five", "hundred", "ninety-three", "thirty", "ninety-nine", "fifty-three". 50,005: "fifty", "thousand", "five", "hundred", "fifteen", "zero". 26,050: "twenty-six", "thousand", "fifty", "hundred", "five", "sixty-two". 81,200: "eighty-one", "thousand", "two", "hundred", "eighteen", "twenty", "zero". Guess: as in Star Challenge 3. Results: "Thirty-nine thousand five hundred ninety-three", "Fifty thousand five", "Twenty-six thousand fifty", "Eighty-one thousand two hundred". Why for 50,005: "Only the Ones place holds a digit after the thousands, so we say fifty thousand five." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- The child splits every number at the comma: the part before it is said with "thousand", the last three digits are said as hundreds, tens and ones. Tokens show that a column with no token holds 0 and has no word. The child says: "Say the part before the comma and add thousand. A zero holds a place, but we do not say it."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the strip turns green, the board reads the name, the chart columns light one by one, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce and the card says "Well read!"
- Mistake: uses the "zero" card -> red strip, small shake, "A zero holds a place, but we do not say it. Skip that place." The zero column pulses.
- Mistake: leaves out "thousand" -> "Say thousand after the part before the comma." The comma pulses.
- Mistake: reads the digits before the comma one by one -> "Read the part before the comma as one number." That part pulses.
- Mistake: "sixty" for 16, "sixteen" for 60 or "eighty" for 18 -> "Look at the Tens and Ones columns together." The T and O columns pulse.
- Mistake: says "hundred" when the Hundreds column holds 0 -> "The Hundreds column holds 0, so no hundred is said." The H column pulses.
- Mistake: words in the wrong order -> "Say the thousands part first, then the hundreds, tens and ones."
- Hints: (1) "Which part of the number comes before the comma? Say it first." (2) The part before the comma lights up on the board and the matching cards glow in the tray. (3) The first two cards are placed in the strip, for 21,436: "twenty-one", "thousand". In the token challenges: (1) "Count the tokens of each kind." (2) The tokens of one kind light up in their column. (3) The first two digits are placed.
- Edge cases: 10,599 has 0 in Th, so "ten thousand" has no extra word for the 0. 45,045 uses "forty-five" twice. 50,005 and 81,200 leave places silent. In the token challenges the digit 0 is always placed.
7. Ending
- Star Challenge 1 is done when both rows are right, Star Challenge 2 when all 4 rows are right, Star Challenges 3 and 4 when all 4 names in each are built correctly.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Say the part before the comma and add thousand. Then say the hundreds, tens and ones." "A zero holds a place, but we do not say it." Think and talk: "How would you read 40,040 aloud? Which places do you skip?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: dark station wall with a departure board (code-drawn dot-matrix digits); rounded tokens, 10,000 purple, 1,000 green, 100 orange, 10 blue, 1 pink; place value chart; cream word cards; digit tiles 0 to 9; speaker icon. English only.

tool_config.idea: Build a number from its name by dropping digit tiles into the TTh, Th, H, T and O slots of a ticket, with a 0 in every place the name skips.
tool_config.title: Number Construction
tool_config.screen: A ticket-printing counter in a warm 3D ticket office with soft shadows and gentle animation. A big blank ticket lies on the counter with five large slots labelled TTh, Th, H, T and O and a comma gap before the last three slots; the slots and the number name are the largest things on screen. The number name sits on a strip above the ticket in large type (for example Ten thousand ten). A tray of digit tiles 0 to 9 sits below. Controls: drag a digit tile into a slot, tap a slot to clear it, a Print ticket button that checks the ticket, a Read it back button that shows how the ticket reads as a name, Back and Next in the same places on every card, a Hint button, a Reset button and progress dots. Read-outs: the worth of each placed digit under its slot (for example a 3 in the T slot reads 30), the ticket number with its comma, and a counter of the card number out of 7.
feedback: A digit tile in a slot shows its worth under it, for example a 3 in the T slot reads 30.
Pressing Print ticket with an empty slot makes the slot blink and says this place needs a digit, use 0 if the name skips it.
A ticket that does not match the name shows the name that the ticket reads as, next to the name asked for, so the student sees the difference without being told the digit.
A correct ticket prints with a stamp and the comma in place before the last three digits.

media.instructions_for_student: The student writes a number from its name by putting each digit in its own place and a 0 in every place the name skips.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Number Construction
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S8.T8.C21.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: We the Travellers - I, Let Us Do Question 2, the name-to-number half: Ten thousand seven hundred forty-three to Thirty-six thousand one (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student writes a number from its name by placing each digit in its own place and putting 0 in every place the name skips.
- Out of scope: reading a number aloud, comparing numbers, numbers beyond 5 digits, expanded form.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A wooden railway booking counter with a brass stamp. A big cream ticket lies on it, about 70% of the stage width, with five large empty slots labelled TTh, Th, H, T, O and a comma gap between Th and H. Above the ticket a strip shows the name: "Thirty-four thousand two hundred twelve".
- Under each slot is a small read-out line for the worth of the digit placed there. Below the counter is a tray of digit tiles 0 to 9.
- Instruction line: "Write the number for this name."
- The child is invited to touch the first slot.
2. Scene and Objects
- Slots are about 12% of the stage width each. The comma is already printed in Activities 1 and 2. From Activity 3 on, the comma is a tile "," in the tray that must be dropped in a gap; the ticket then has 4 small gaps, one between each pair of slots.
- Goal chips on the stage: "Print the ticket" in the Activities, "Tickets: 0 of 3" in the practice and the stars.
- Worth lines show for example "30" under a 3 in the T slot. They are hidden from Activity 3 on.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a digit tile into a slot. Tiles stay in the tray when used. Tap a slot to clear it. A tile dropped on a filled slot replaces the digit.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" and one big "Check" button that becomes "Next" when the pill is done. "Check" prints the ticket with a stamp when it is right and also reads the ticket back as a name.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Write the number for this name." Goal chip: "Print the ticket". Name: "Thirty-four thousand two hundred twelve". Guess: the child taps how many digits the number has ("4", "5" or "6"); the answer is 5. Then the child drops 3, 4, 2, 1, 2. Result: the ticket prints 34,212. Why: "Thirty-four thousand gives TTh 3 and Th 4. Two hundred twelve gives H 2, T 1, O 2: 30,000 + 4,000 + 200 + 10 + 2 = 34,212." Help: guided, worth lines shown, the words of the name glow in the colour of their slots.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Fill every place. Use 0 where the name skips a place." Goal chip: "Print the ticket". Name: "Twenty-five thousand six". Guess: the child taps one of three printed tickets: "2,506", "25,006" or "25,060". Then the child builds the ticket. Result: 25,006 prints. Why: "Twenty-five thousand gives TTh 2 and Th 5. No hundreds and no tens, so H and T hold 0, and 6 is in Ones: 25,006." Help: guided, worth lines shown, empty slots blink.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Write the number. Do not forget the comma." Goal chip: "Print the ticket". Name: "Eighty thousand three hundred". Guess: before dropping digits, the child taps the slots that will hold 0 (Th, T and O) and a small "0?" mark sits on each. Then the child fills the slots and drops the comma tile. Result: 80,300 prints. Why: "Eighty gives TTh 8 and Th 0, three hundred gives H 3, and nothing is said for Tens and Ones, so they hold 0: 80,300." Help: independent, worth lines hidden.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Write the number. Do not forget the comma." Goal chip: "Print the ticket". Name: "Sixty-three thousand seventy". Guess: the child taps the slots that will hold 0 (H and O). Result: 63,070 prints. Why: "Sixty-three gives TTh 6 and Th 3. After it only seventy is said, so T is 7 and H and O hold 0: 63,070." Help: independent.
- Practice (independent), three quick tickets. Goal line: "Write the number for each name." Goal chip: "Tickets: 0 of 3". Names: "Ninety-two thousand four hundred one", "Fourteen thousand five", "Seventy-eight thousand sixty-two". Guess: the child taps the zero slots first, as in Activity 3. Results: 92,401 (T holds 0), 14,005 (H and T hold 0) and 78,062 (H holds 0). Why for the second: "Fourteen thousand gives 1 and 4. Only 5 is said after it, so H and T hold 0: 14,005." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "Fill in the blanks appropriately. Use commas as required. Write the number for each of these names." Goal chip: "Tickets: 0 of 3". Names: "Ten thousand seven hundred forty-three", "Ten thousand ten", "Fifty-six thousand four hundred ninety-one". Answers 10,743; 10,010; 56,491. Guess: the child taps the zero slots first. Why for 10,010: "Ten thousand gives TTh 1 and Th 0. Ten gives T 1, so H and O hold 0: 10,010." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Same goal line. Goal chip: "Tickets: 0 of 3". Names: "Ninety thousand nine", "Twenty-three thousand two hundred thirty", "Thirty-six thousand one". Answers 90,009; 23,230; 36,001. Guess: the child taps the zero slots first. Why for 90,009: "Ninety thousand gives TTh 9 and Th 0. Nine gives O 9, so H and T hold 0: 90,009." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- The word "thousand" splits the name. The part before it fills TTh and Th. The part after it fills H, T and O. A place the name does not mention holds 0, so all five places are always filled. The child says: "Find the word thousand. Put 0 in every place the name skips."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the ticket prints with the stamp, the comma sits before the last three digits, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce and the strip says "Ticket printed!"
- Mistake: a slot left empty -> red strip, small shake, "Every place needs a digit. Use 0 where the name skips a place." The empty slot pulses.
- Mistake: a ticket that reads as a different name, such as 2,506 for the name in Activity 2 -> "Your ticket reads: two thousand five hundred six. Look at the places that hold 0." Both names show, one under the other.
- Mistake: digits in the wrong places, such as 36,010 for "Thirty-six thousand one" -> "Your ticket reads: thirty-six thousand ten. Look at which place holds the 1." The T and O slots pulse.
- Mistake: comma in the wrong gap -> "The comma goes before the last three digits." The gap between Th and H pulses.
- Mistake: 0 in the TTh slot -> "A 5-digit number does not start with 0. The first digit of the part before thousand goes here." The TTh slot pulses.
- Hints: (1) "Which word in the name tells you where the thousands end?" (2) The word "thousand" glows in the name and the comma gap lights between Th and H. (3) The first two digits are placed in TTh and Th.
- Edge cases: names like "Ninety thousand nine" skip three places. "Ten thousand ten" has 0 in Th. A name that ends in "thousand" such as "Twenty thousand" would leave all of H, T and O as 0.
7. Ending
- Practice is done when all 3 tickets are right. Star Challenges 1 and 2 are done when all 3 tickets in each are right.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Find the word thousand. The part before it goes in TTh and Th." "Put 0 in every place the name skips." Think and talk: "Why is fifty thousand twelve written 50,012 and not 5,012?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: wooden booking counter photo; cream railway ticket with 5 slots and a comma gap; brass stamp; digit tiles 0 to 9 and a comma tile; printed small tickets for the Activity 2 guess. English only.

content.text:
1. Predict first: 120, 135, 150. What is added each time, and what comes next?
2. Find the jump between neighbours: 135 − 120 = 15 and 150 − 135 = 15. The jump is the same, so the rule is add 15.
3. The next number is 150 + 15 = 165. Test the rule on every pair, not only the first two. If one jump is different, the rule is wrong.
4. Rule: a pattern adds or subtracts the same number each time. Find that number and use it.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the rule and write the next two numbers: 2,150, 2,450, 2,750, 3,050.
1. Subtract each number from the one after it: 2,450 − 2,150 = 300.
2. 2,750 − 2,450 = 300.
3. 3,050 − 2,750 = 300.
4. The jump is the same every time, so the rule is add 300.
5. The next number is 3,050 + 300 = 3,350.
6. Then 3,350 + 300 = 3,650.
7. Check: 2,150 to 3,650 is 5 jumps, and 5 × 300 = 1,500, so 2,150 + 1,500 = 3,650.
Answer: The rule is add 300, and the next numbers are 3,350 and 3,650

media.title: Which number is greater?
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Students compare two numbers by counting their digits first, and when the digits are equal they compare place by place from the left, to say which number is greater. It works this example: Which is greater, 8,965 or 21,304? Then which is greater, 47,260 or 47,620?

video_script.why: Students compare two numbers by counting their digits first, and when the digits are equal they compare place by place from the left, to say which number is greater.
source: Which is greater, 8,965 or 21,304? Then which is greater, 47
video_script.status: placeholder: the script and the video are made in the media folders
hold_back: 21,304 is greater than 8,965, and 47,620 is greater than 47,260

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: which is greater, 8,965 or 21,304? The first digit 8 is bigger than 2. Does that decide it? Count the digits first. 8,965 has 4 digits and 21,304 has 5 digits. A number with more digits is greater. The 8 in 8,965 is only 8 Thousands, but the 2 in 21,304 is 2 Ten Thousands, worth 20,000. When both numbers have the same number of digits, compare from the left, place by place. Stop at the first place where the digits are different. The bigger digit there makes the greater number. Rule: count the digits first. If they are equal, compare from the left. 1. 8,965 has 4 digits and 21,304 has 5 digits. 2. The number with more digits is greater, so 21,304 is greater than 8,965, even though 8 is bigger than 2. 3. 47,260 and 47,620 both have 5 digits, so compare place by place from the left. 4. The TTh digits are 4 and 4, equal. The Th digits are 7 and 7, equal. The H digits are 2 and 6, different, so stop here. 5. 6 is greater than 2, so 47,620 is greater than 47,260. Answer: 21,304 is greater than 8,965, and 47,620 is greater than 47,260

topics.summary: A number with more digits is greater. With the same number of digits, compare from the left, place by place. On a number line the greater number is farther to the right, and many numbers lie between any two numbers.

content.text:
1. Predict first: which is greater, 8,965 or 21,304? The first digit 8 is bigger than 2. Does that decide it?
2. Count the digits first. 8,965 has 4 digits and 21,304 has 5 digits.
3. A number with more digits is greater. The 8 in 8,965 is only 8 Thousands, but the 2 in 21,304 is 2 Ten Thousands, worth 20,000.
4. When both numbers have the same number of digits, compare from the left, place by place. Stop at the first place where the digits are different. The bigger digit there makes the greater number.
5. Rule: count the digits first. If they are equal, compare from the left.

content.text:
Worked example: Which is greater, 8,965 or 21,304? Then which is greater, 47,260 or 47,620?
1. 8,965 has 4 digits and 21,304 has 5 digits.
2. The number with more digits is greater, so 21,304 is greater than 8,965, even though 8 is bigger than 2.
3. 47,260 and 47,620 both have 5 digits, so compare place by place from the left.
4. The TTh digits are 4 and 4, equal. The Th digits are 7 and 7, equal. The H digits are 2 and 6, different, so stop here.
5. 6 is greater than 2, so 47,620 is greater than 47,260.
Answer: 21,304 is greater than 8,965, and 47,620 is greater than 47,260

content.text:
1. All eight numbers have $5$ digits, so compare the ten thousands digits first: $4$, $3$, $4$, $3$, $7$, $7$, $4$ and $1$.
2. Ten thousands digit $1$: $18,926$. It is the smallest.
3. Ten thousands digit $3$: $34,407$ and $34,740$. The thousands digits are $4$ and $4$, so compare the hundreds digits, $4$ and $7$. $34,407$ is smaller.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution]
4. Ten thousands digit $4$: $40,347$, $40,473$ and $47,340$. The thousands digits are $0$, $0$ and $7$, so $47,340$ is the greatest of the three.
5. Compare the hundreds digits of the other two, $3$ and $4$. $40,347$ is smaller than $40,473$.
6. Ten thousands digit $7$: $73,404$ and $74,430$. The thousands digits are $3$ and $4$, so $73,404$ is smaller.
7. Check: on the number line from $0$ to $80,000$ the eight numbers also sit from left to right in this order.
Answer: $18,926$; $34,407$; $34,740$; $40,347$; $40,473$; $47,340$; $73,404$; $74,430$

content.text:
1. Write both numbers in the place value chart. $9,990$ is $9$ thousands, $9$ hundreds, $9$ tens and $0$ ones. It has $4$ digits and the ten thousands place is empty.
2. $49,014$ is $4$ ten thousands, $9$ thousands, $0$ hundreds, $1$ tens and $4$ ones. It has $5$ digits.
3. A number with more digits is greater, so $49,014$ is greater than $9,990$.
[Image: Let us do: Ans2: solution]
4. The student compared $9$ with $4$, but the $9$ in $9,990$ is in the thousands place and the $4$ in $49,014$ is in the ten thousands place. Compare first digits only when both numbers have the same number of digits.
5. Fill the number line. The marks are $5,000$ apart, so $10,000 - 5,000 = 5,000$ and $50,000 - 45,000 = 5,000$.
6. The blank marks are $15,000$, $20,000$, $25,000$, $30,000$, $35,000$, $40,000$ and $45,000$.
7. $9,990$ sits just before the $10,000$ mark. $49,014$ sits just before the $50,000$ mark, much farther to the right.
8. Check: $49,014$ is farther to the right than $9,990$, so it is greater.

steps_tex: Write both numbers in the place value chart. $9,990$ is $9$ thousands, $9$ hundreds, $9$ tens and $0$ ones. It has $4$ digits and the ten thousands place is empty.
$49,014$ is $4$ ten thousands, $9$ thousands, $0$ hundreds, $1$ tens and $4$ ones. It has $5$ digits.
A number with more digits is greater, so $49,014$ is greater than $9,990$.

The student compared $9$ with $4$, but the $9$ in $9,990$ is in the thousands place and the $4$ in $49,014$ is in the ten thousands place. Compare first digits only when both numbers have the same number of digits.
Fill the number line. The marks are $5,000$ apart, so $10,000 - 5,000 = 5,000$ and $50,000 - 45,000 = 5,000$.
$9,990$ sits just before the $10,000$ mark. $49,014$ sits just before the $50,000$ mark, much farther to the right.
Check: $49,014$ is farther to the right than $9,990$, so it is greater.
content.answer_tex: No, the student is not correct. $49,014$ is greater than $9,990$ because it has $5$ digits and $9,990$ has $4$. The blanks are $15,000$, $20,000$, $25,000$, $30,000$, $35,000$, $40,000$ and $45,000$.

content.publication_text: Write $5$ numbers between the numbers $23,568$ and $24,234$.

content.text:
1. A number between them must be greater than $23,568$ and less than $24,234$.
2. Both numbers have $5$ digits and start with $2$. The thousands digits are $3$ and $4$.
3. With thousands digit $3$ and a bigger hundreds digit, $23,600$ and $23,800$ are greater than $23,568$.
4. With thousands digit $4$ and a small hundreds digit, $24,000$, $24,100$ and $24,200$ are less than $24,234$.
5. Choose five of them: $23,600$, $23,800$, $24,000$, $24,100$ and $24,200$.
6. Check: $23,568$ is less than $23,600$, and $24,200$ is less than $24,234$.
Answer: Sample answer: $23,600$; $23,800$; $24,000$; $24,100$ and $24,200$. Your answer may differ.

content.question_tex: Write $5$ numbers that are more than $38,125$ but less than $38,600$.
content.publication_text: Write $5$ numbers that are more than $38,125$ but less than $38,600$.

content.text:
1. The numbers must be greater than $38,125$ and less than $38,600$.
2. All of them start with $38$, so only the hundreds, tens and ones change. A hundreds digit from $2$ to $5$ is safe: every such number is greater than $38,125$ and less than $38,600$.
3. $38,200$, $38,300$, $38,400$ and $38,500$ use the hundreds digits $2$, $3$, $4$ and $5$.
4. $38,599$ is also less than $38,600$, because $38,599 + 1 = 38,600$.
5. Check: the smallest, $38,200$, is greater than $38,125$, and the biggest, $38,599$, is less than $38,600$.
Answer: Sample answer: $38,200$; $38,300$; $38,400$; $38,500$ and $38,599$. Your answer may differ.

Answer: Sheetal's car, $67,543\text{ km}$, has been driven more.

content.text:
1. All six prices have $5$ digits. Compare the ten thousands digits: $9$, $8$, $9$, $4$, $9$ and $3$.
2. The smallest ten thousands digit is $3$, so ₹$39,999$ is first. Then $4$ gives ₹$49,900$ and $8$ gives ₹$89,999$.
3. Three prices have ten thousands digit $9$: ₹$90,000$, ₹$94,983$ and ₹$93,743$. Compare their thousands digits: $0$, $4$ and $3$.
4. $0$ is less than $3$ and $3$ is less than $4$, so the order is ₹$90,000$, ₹$93,743$, ₹$94,983$.
5. Put the parts together: ₹$39,999$, ₹$49,900$, ₹$89,999$, then ₹$90,000$, ₹$93,743$ and ₹$94,983$.
6. Check: $89,999 + 1 = 90,000$, so ₹$89,999$ comes just before ₹$90,000$.
Answer: ₹$39,999$; ₹$49,900$; ₹$89,999$; ₹$90,000$; ₹$93,743$; ₹$94,983$

6. Check: $66,540$, $65,232$, $56,380$, $53,231$, $51,336$ and $45,858$ each get smaller.
Answer: Town $6$: $66,540$, Town $1$: $65,232$, Town $3$: $56,380$, Town $2$: $53,231$, Town $4$: $51,336$, Town $5$: $45,858$

content.question_tex: Find numbers between $42,750$ and $53,500$ such that the ones, tens, and hundreds digits are all $0$.
content.publication_text: Find numbers between $42,750$ and $53,500$ such that the ones, tens, and hundreds digits are all $0$.

content.text:
1. A number with $0$ in the ones, tens and hundreds places is a whole number of thousands, like $43,000$.
2. The first such number after $42,750$ is $43,000$, because $42,000$ is less than $42,750$.
3. The last such number before $53,500$ is $53,000$, because $54,000$ is more than $53,500$.
4. List them by adding $1,000$ each time: $43,000$, $44,000$, $45,000$, $46,000$, $47,000$, $48,000$, $49,000$, $50,000$, $51,000$, $52,000$ and $53,000$.
5. Count them: $53 - 43 + 1 = 11$ numbers.
[Image: Let us do: Ans8: solution]
6. Check: every number has $0$ in the ones, tens and hundreds places, and all lie between $42,750$ and $53,500$.
Answer: $43,000$; $44,000$; $45,000$; $46,000$; $47,000$; $48,000$; $49,000$; $50,000$; $51,000$; $52,000$ and $53,000$: $11$ numbers in all
[Image: Let us do: Ans8: solution (continued)]

tool_config.idea: Swapping two digits of a number moves each digit into the other digit's place, so each one takes a new value and the number changes. The student swaps two coaches of a number train, compares the old number with the new number, and chooses swaps to reach a target.
tool_config.title: Digit Swap Challenge
tool_config.screen: A warm, colourful 3D and isometric station with one short railway track, soft shadows and gentle animation. The number train is the largest thing on the screen: each digit of the number is one big coach on the track, the place name (TTh, Th, H, T, O) is painted under each coach, and the whole number with its comma is written large above the train. Below the track two number cards sit side by side, Before and After, with a line that says bigger, smaller or the same and shows the change in value. The task of the card is one short sentence above the train. Controls, all large: tap a coach to select it (a selected coach glows and shows 1 or 2), Swap (the two coaches glide past each other), Undo, Reset, Check, Hint, Back and Next in the same place on every card, and a row of progress dots, one for each of the 6 cards.
feedback: After every swap the Before and After cards show both numbers with their place chart, and a line says bigger, smaller or the same together with the change in value, for example 3,600 more.
Two coaches with the same digit show 'These two digits are the same, so the number stays the same.'
A swap that would put 0 at the front shows 'A number cannot start with 0. Try another swap.' and the coaches slide back.
A swap that does not meet the card shows the new number beside the task, for example 'This number is 30,591. The task needs more than 35,000.', and Undo glows.

A correct swap makes the train glow green and names the swap that was made, such as 'You swapped 5 and 2.' If the card has more than one right swap, it adds 'Another swap also works. Can you find it?'
Reset puts the train back to its first number; Back and Next never lose the work on a finished card.
tool_config.done_when: All 6 cards are done with a correct swap, and the student has made at least one swap that made a number bigger and one that made a number smaller.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1: the train shows 2,614. Swap the coaches 2 and 6 and compare the new number with 2,614. Answer: 6,214, which is bigger, because 6,214 − 2,614 = 3,600.

Card 2: the train shows 4,552. Swap the two coaches that hold the digit 5, then swap the coach 4 with the first coach 5. Answer: the first swap leaves 4,552 as it was, because the two digits are the same; the second swap gives 5,452, which is bigger.
Card 3: the train shows 36,172. Make the biggest number you can with one swap, then the smallest. Answer: biggest 76,132 (swap 3 and 7); smallest 16,372 (swap 3 and 1).
Card 4: the train shows 52,430. Swap two coaches to make a number between 25,000 and 30,000. Answer: 25,430 (swap 5 and 2).

Challenge card 1: (a) In the number 1,478, interchanging the digits 7 and 4 gives 1,748. Now, interchange any two digits in the number 1,478 to make a number that is larger than 5,500. (b) Interchange two digits of 10,593 to make a number (i) between 11,000 and 15,000 (ii) more than 35,000. Answer: (a) 7,418 or 8,471; (b)(i) 13,590; (b)(ii) 50,193 or 90,513.
Challenge card 2: (c) Interchange two digits of 48,247 to make a number (i) as small as possible (ii) as big as possible. Answer: (i) 28,447; (ii) 84,247.

hint_ladder.text: Which place must change for the number to get bigger or smaller? Look at the leftmost coaches first.
A bigger digit in a bigger place makes the number bigger. A smaller digit in that place makes it smaller.
Tap the coach with the digit you want to move and the coach whose place you want to change, press Swap and read the After card.
To make 7,358 bigger, bring the 8 to the thousands place: swap 7 and 8 to get 8,357. Now try the next card.

media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Digit Swap Challenge
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S14.T14.C55.2D1
- Tool type: Puzzle
- Textbook source: We the Travellers - I, Let Us Do Question 5, Digit swap: 1,478 (larger than 5,500), 10,593 (between 11,000 and 15,000, more than 35,000) and 48,247 (as small as possible, as big as possible) (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that swapping two different digits changes the value of both digits and so changes the number, and uses this to make a number bigger, smaller, in a range, the biggest or the smallest.
- Out of scope: swapping more than two digits, rearranging all digits, rounding, comparing numbers of different lengths.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A short railway track in a station yard. A number train stands on it: each digit of the number is one big coach, painted in a different colour, with a digit on its side. The first train carries 2,714, so it has 4 coaches, each about 14% of the stage width. A sign under each coach names its place: Th, H, T, O. Above the train the whole number is written large with its comma: 2,714.
- Below the track two cards sit side by side: "Before" showing 2,714 and "After" empty, with a line between them for "bigger", "smaller" or "the same".
- Instruction line: "Swap the 2 and the 7. Will the number get bigger, smaller or stay the same?"
- The child is invited to tap the first coach.
2. Scene and Objects
- A selected coach glows and shows a small 1 or 2 badge. Worth labels under the coaches (2,000, 700, 10, 4) show in guided activities only. The Before and After cards show the number with a mini place chart.
- Goal chips on the stage: "Swap 1", "Swap 2", "Smaller", "Biggest and smallest", "Between 30,000 and 40,000" in the Activities, and the target of the question in the stars, such as "More than 5,500".
3. Main Interaction
- Tap two coaches to select them. In Activities 1 to 3 and the stars, three prediction chips then appear: "Bigger", "Smaller", "Same". When the child taps one, the two coaches glide past each other and swap places, the whole number updates and the After card shows. In Activities 4 and 5 the guess is the first tap on the digit to bring to the front, and the swap happens when the second coach is tapped. Tap a selected coach again to unselect it.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Undo" and "Next". "Undo" steps back one swap; pressing it again goes further back to the first number. "Next" is greyed out until the goal chip is green.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Swap the 2 and the 7. Will the number get bigger, smaller or stay the same?" Goal chip: "Swap 1". Train 2,714, the coaches 2 and 7 pulse. Guess: the child taps "Bigger", "Smaller" or "Same". Result: the train shows 7,214 and the After card says "bigger by 4,500". Why: "The 7 grew from 700 to 7,000 and the 2 shrank from 2,000 to 200. 7,000 − 700 = 6,300 more and 2,000 − 200 = 1,800 less, so 6,300 − 1,800 = 4,500 more: 7,214 − 2,714 = 4,500." Help: guided, worth labels and arrows show where each digit goes.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Swap the two 4s. Then swap the 8 with the first 4." Goal chip: "Swap 2". Train 8,445. Guess: the child taps a prediction chip before each swap. Result: the first swap leaves 8,445 and the After card says "the same"; the second swap shows 4,845, "smaller by 3,600". Why: "Two digits that are the same change nothing. The 4 grew from 400 to 4,000, which is 3,600 more, and the 8 shrank from 8,000 to 800, which is 7,200 less: 7,200 − 3,600 = 3,600 less. 8,445 − 4,845 = 3,600." Help: guided, worth labels shown.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Make a smaller number with one swap." Goal chip: "Smaller". Train 5,792, no labels. Guess: the child taps a prediction chip before the swap. Result: the swaps 5 and 2 (2,795), 7 and 2 (5,297) or 9 and 2 (5,729) all work; the strip says "You swapped 5 and 2. The bigger digit moved to a smaller place: 5,792 became 2,795, which is 2,997 less." Other numbers use the same sentence with their own numbers, 495 less for 5,297 and 63 less for 5,729. Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Make the biggest number you can with one swap. Then the smallest." Goal chip: "Biggest and smallest". Train 41,968. Guess: before selecting coaches, the child taps the digit to bring to the front; the tapped coach glows. Result: biggest 91,468 (swap 4 and 9); then the train resets to 41,968 and the smallest is 14,968 (swap 4 and 1). Why: "The TTh place is worth the most. Bring the biggest digit 9 there to get 91,468. Bring the smallest digit 1 there to get 14,968." Help: independent.
- Activity 5 (independent). Goal line: "Make a number between 30,000 and 40,000 with one swap." Goal chip: "Between 30,000 and 40,000". Train 63,208. Guess: the child taps the digit that must stand in the TTh place (the answer is 3). Result: swap 6 and 3 gives 36,208, the only swap that works. Why: "The TTh digit must be 3. 36,208 is more than 30,000 and less than 40,000." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "In the number 1,478, interchanging the digits 7 and 4 gives 1,748. Now, interchange any two digits in the number 1,478 to make a number that is larger than 5,500." Goal chip: "More than 5,500". Train 1,478. The first swap of 7 and 4 plays by itself to show 1,748. Guess: a prediction chip before each swap. Result: swap 1 and 7 gives 7,418; swap 1 and 8 gives 8,471. Why: "The Thousands digit must be 5 or more. Swapping 1 with 7 or 8 gives 7,418 or 8,471, both more than 5,500." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "Interchange two digits of 10,593 to make a number between 11,000 and 15,000. Then make a number more than 35,000." Goal chips: "11,000 to 15,000" and "More than 35,000". Train 10,593; it resets after part (i). Guess: a prediction chip before each swap. Result (i): swap 0 and 3 gives 13,590, the only way. Result (ii): swap 1 and 5 gives 50,193 and swap 1 and 9 gives 90,513. Why: "(i) Keep 1 in TTh and bring 3 to Th: 13,590. (ii) Bring a bigger digit to TTh: 50,193 or 90,513 are more than 35,000." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "Interchange two digits of 48,247 to make a number as small as possible. Then as big as possible." Goal chips: "As small as possible" and "As big as possible". Train 48,247. Guess: a prediction chip before each swap. Result: smallest 28,447 (swap 4 and 2); biggest 84,247 (swap 4 and 8). Why: "Bring the smallest digit 2 to TTh: 28,447. Bring the biggest digit 8 to TTh: 84,247." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Each digit has a value from its place. When two different digits swap, each takes the other's place and its value changes, so the number changes. A bigger digit moving to a bigger place makes the number bigger. The child says: "Swapping two different digits changes the number. The leftmost place matters most."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the train glows green, the strip names the swap ("You swapped 5 and 2. Nice swap!"), the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce. If another swap also works the strip adds "Another swap also works. Can you find it?"
- Mistake: prediction does not match -> red strip, small shake, "You said bigger, but the number got smaller: the bigger digit moved to a smaller place." The same line is used for each mismatch with the child's word and the real result. The coaches that swapped pulse.
- Mistake: the swap does not meet the task -> "This number is 30,591. The task needs more than 35,000." The task chip pulses and Undo glows.
- Mistake: swapping with a 0 to the front, such as 1 and 0 in 10,593 -> "A number cannot start with 0. Try another swap." The coaches slide back.
- Mistake: two equal digits -> "These two digits are the same, so the number stays the same." Both coaches pulse.
- Mistake: smaller but not the smallest (42,847 in Star Challenge 3) -> "42,847 is smaller. Can you make it even smaller? Look at the TTh place." The TTh coach pulses.
- Hints: (1) "Which place matters most for the size of the number? Look at the leftmost coach." (2) The leftmost coach glows and small arrows point to the digits that could go there. (3) The two coaches to swap are selected for the child.
- Edge cases: in 8,445 and 48,247 two digits are the same. In 10,593 and 63,208 the 0 must stay away from the front. Activity 3, Star Challenge 1 and Star Challenge 2 (ii) have more than one right swap; Activity 5 and Star Challenge 2 (i) have exactly one.
7. Ending
- Activities 1 and 2 are done when both swaps are made. Activity 3 is done with any swap that makes the number smaller. Activity 4 is done when both the biggest and the smallest are made. Activity 5 is done with 36,208. Star Challenges are done when every part meets its task.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Swapping two different digits changes the number." "A bigger digit moving to a bigger place makes the number bigger." "For the biggest number bring the biggest digit to the front. For the smallest, bring the smallest digit, but never 0." Think and talk: "Why can you not bring the 0 of 30,572 to the front to make a smaller number?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: station yard track; train coaches in 5 colours with a digit on each side (code-drawn); place signs Th, H, T, O and TTh; "Before" and "After" number cards; small arrows. English only.

After the swap, each digit stands in the other digit's place, so its value changes. In 3,925 the 9 is worth 900. After the swap it stands in the thousands place and is worth 9,000. topics.summary: Each digit has a place, and the place gives its value. When two different digits swap, both change their value and the number changes. A bigger digit in a bigger place makes a bigger number.

content.text:
1. Predict first: in 3,925, swap the digits 3 and 9. Will the new number be the same, bigger or smaller?
2. Each digit has a place, and the place gives its value. After the swap, each digit stands in the other digit's place, so its value changes.
3. In 3,925 the 9 is worth 900. After the swap it stands in the thousands place and is worth 9,000. The 3 was worth 3,000 and is now worth 300.
4. Swapping two different digits always changes the number. Swapping two digits that are the same changes nothing.
5. Rule: a bigger digit moving to a bigger place makes the number bigger.

content.text:
Worked example: Swap the digits 3 and 9 in 3,925. Write the new number and say how it compares with 3,925.
1. 3,925 = 3 Thousands + 9 Hundreds + 2 Tens + 5 Ones.
2. Swap the 3 and the 9. The 9 moves to the thousands place and the 3 moves to the hundreds place. The new number is 9,325.
3. The 9 was worth 900 and is now worth 9,000. It gained 9,000 − 900 = 8,100.

content.text:
1. Predict first: in 62,815, which digit should stand in the ten thousands place to make the number as big as it can be?
2. The ten thousands place has the greatest value, so look at it first.
3. To make the biggest number with one swap, bring the biggest digit to the leftmost place. To make the smallest number, bring the smallest digit there.
4. A number cannot start with 0, so never bring a 0 to the front.
5. If the biggest digit is already at the front, leave it and look at the next place.

content.text:
Worked example: Swap two digits of 62,815 to make (a) the biggest number and (b) the smallest number you can with one swap.
1. 62,815 has the digits 6, 2, 8, 1 and 5. The leftmost place, the ten thousands place, matters most.
2. (a) Biggest: the biggest digit is 8. Bring it to the ten thousands place by swapping 6 and 8. The new number is 82,615.
3. (b) Smallest: the smallest digit is 1. Bring it to the ten thousands place by swapping 6 and 1. The new number is 12,865.
4. Check: 82,615 is more than 62,815 and 12,865 is less than 62,815.
Answer: (a) 82,615 (swap 6 and 8). (b) 12,865 (swap 6 and 1).

content.text:
1. $(a)$: To be larger than $5,500$, the thousands digit must be $5$ or more. $1,478$ has $1$ in the thousands place, and its digits are $1$, $4$, $7$ and $8$.
2. Bring $7$ or $8$ to the thousands place: swap $1$ and $7$ to get $7,418$, or swap $1$ and $8$ to get $8,471$.
3. $(b)$(i): For a number between $11,000$ and $15,000$, keep $1$ in the ten thousands place and put $1$, $2$, $3$ or $4$ in the thousands place. $10,593$ has $0$ in the thousands place, so swap $0$ and $3$ to get $13,590$.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution]
4. Swapping $0$ with $5$ gives $15,093$ and swapping $0$ with $9$ gives $19,503$, both too big. So $13,590$ is the only way.
5. $(b)$(ii): The ten thousands digit of $10,593$ is $1$. Swapping $1$ and $3$ gives only $30,591$, which is less than $35,000$.
6. Bring a bigger digit to the ten thousands place: swap $1$ and $5$ to get $50,193$, or swap $1$ and $9$ to get $90,513$. Both are more than $35,000$.
7. $(c)$(i): $48,247$ has the digits $4$, $8$, $2$, $4$ and $7$. For the smallest number, bring the smallest digit, $2$, to the ten thousands place by swapping $4$ and $2$. The new number is $28,447$.
8. $(c)$(ii): For the biggest number, bring the biggest digit, $8$, to the ten thousands place by swapping $4$ and $8$. The new number is $84,247$.
9. Check: $7,418$ is more than $5,500$; $13,590$ is between $11,000$ and $15,000$; $50,193$ is more than $35,000$; $28,447$ is less than $48,247$ and $84,247$ is more than $48,247$.
Answer: $(a)$: $7,418$ or $8,471$. $(b)$(i): $13,590$. $(b)$(ii): $50,193$ or $90,513$. $(c)$(i): $28,447$. $(c)$(ii): $84,247$.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution (continued)]

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many ₹10 notes are there in ₹574? Is it the tens digit, 7?
2. No. One ₹10 note is 10, so count how many tens fit. 50 tens make 500 and 7 more tens make 70, so there are 57 tens in 574, with 4 ones left.
3. To count the tens, drop the ones digit. To count the hundreds, drop the last two digits. To count the thousands, drop the last three digits.
4. The same number can be grouped in more than one way. 574 = 57 Tens + 4 Ones, and also 50 Tens + 74 Ones. The number does not change.
5. Two ₹500 notes make 1,000, so count the thousands and double them. Then see if the rest holds one more 500.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the number of tens, hundreds and thousands in 2,745. Write 2,745 as 200 Tens + __ Ones. How many ₹500 notes are there in ₹2,745?
1. Tens: 274 × 10 = 2,740 and 2,745 − 2,740 = 5. So there are 274 tens, with 5 ones left.
2. Hundreds: 27 × 100 = 2,700 and 2,745 − 2,700 = 45. So there are 27 hundreds, with 45 left.
3. Thousands: 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 and 2,745 − 2,000 = 745. So there are 2 thousands, with 745 left.
4. 200 Tens is 2,000 and 2,745 − 2,000 = 745, so 2,745 = 200 Tens + 745 Ones.
5. ₹500 notes: 5 hundreds make one ₹500 note. 27 hundreds hold 5 notes, because 5 × 5 = 25 hundreds and 2 hundreds are left over.
6. Check: 5 × 500 = 2,500, which is less than ₹2,745, and 6 × 500 = 3,000, which is more.
Answer: 274 tens, 27 hundreds and 2 thousands; 2,745 = 200 Tens + 745 Ones; 5 notes of ₹500

1. $(a)$: is done: $793 \times 10 = 7,930$ and $7,934 - 7,930 = 4$, so there are $793$ notes of ₹$10$.
2. $(b)$: $79 \times 100 = 7,900$ and $7,934 - 7,900 = 34$, so there are $79$ notes of ₹$100$.
3. $(c)$: $7 \times 1,000 = 7,000$ and $7,934 - 7,000 = 934$, so there are $7$ thousands.
4. $(d)$: Two ₹$500$ notes make $1,000$. From $(c)$, $7$ thousands hold $7 \times 2 = 14$ notes of ₹$500$.
5. The $934$ that is left is more than $500$, so there is one more note: $14 + 1 = 15$.
6. Check: $15 \times 500 = 7,500$, which is less than ₹$7,934$, and $16 \times 500 = 8,000$, which is more.
Answer: $(b)$: $79$ notes; $(c)$: $7$ thousands; $(d)$: $15$ notes of ₹$500$

media.title: Rounding Number Line

tool_config.idea: The nearest ten, hundred or thousand of a number is the neighbouring mark that needs fewer jumps. The student places a rabbit on a milestone road between two neighbouring marks, counts the jumps to each mark and chooses the nearer one.
tool_config.title: Rounding Number Line
tool_config.screen: A warm, colourful 3D and isometric countryside with one milestone road, soft shadows and gentle animation. The target number is the largest text, above the road. The road is a straight path drawn as a number line: a carrot (the food) at each end shows the two neighbouring tens, hundreds or thousands, a lit milestone in the middle shows the halfway number, and the student drags a rabbit marker along the road. Read-outs: under the rabbit the number it stands on, under each carrot the jumps to it (shown once the rabbit is placed), and a line Nearest: ___ that fills in after the choice. Controls, all large: a three-button switch Tens, Hundreds and Thousands, tap a carrot to choose it, Check, Hint, Retry, Reset, Back and Next in the same place on every card, and progress dots, one for each of the 7 cards. Only one road is shown at a time. Every target is nearer to one carrot than to the other, so no card ever puts the rabbit on the halfway milestone.
feedback: Once the rabbit is placed, the jump count appears under each carrot, for example 3 jumps and 7 jumps, and the carrot with fewer jumps starts to glow.
A carrot that needs more jumps shows both counts with 'This carrot needs more jumps. Which carrot needs fewer?', and the rabbit stays so the student can try again.
A rabbit placed on a different number from the one on the card slides back with 'The rabbit is at ___. The card asks for ___.'
A correct choice makes the rabbit hop the jumps one by one with a gentle count, and the nearest number is written on the milestone.

On the three-roads card the road changes after each correct choice and a small row keeps the nearest ten, hundred and thousand found so far, so the student can see that the nearest mark can be below or above the number.
In the table, a box that is not right shows the two neighbours and the jumps to each, so the student can correct it.
tool_config.done_when: All 7 cards are done correctly, and the student has used the Tens, Hundreds and Thousands roads at least once.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

Card 2, nearest ten: the rabbit is at 3,298 and the carrots are at 3,290 and 3,300. Answer: 3,300, 2 jumps (the other carrot needs 8 jumps).
Card 3, nearest hundred: the rabbit is at 4,618 and the carrots are at 4,600 and 4,700. Answer: 4,600, 18 jumps (the other carrot needs 82 jumps).

Card 4, three roads for one number: the rabbit is at 8,327. Switch between the Tens, Hundreds and Thousands roads and choose the nearer carrot on each. Answer: tens 8,330 (3 jumps), hundreds 8,300 (27 jumps), thousands 8,000 (327 jumps).
Card 5, one carrot for two numbers: place the rabbit at 6,298 and then at 6,303 on the Tens road. Answer: both go to 6,300 (2 jumps and 3 jumps), so they have the same nearest ten.

hint_ladder.text: Which two carrots are at the ends of the road, and which one does the rabbit look closer to?
