media.instructions_for_student: The student finds the nearest ten, hundred or thousand of a number by counting the jumps to its two neighbouring marks and choosing the mark with fewer jumps.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Rounding Number Line
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S18.T18.C74.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: We the Travellers - I, Nearest Tens, Hundreds and Thousands: the rabbit at 2,346, the table 3,176, 4,017, 5,789, 8,203, and Let Us Think Questions 1, 2 and 3 (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student finds the nearest ten, hundred or thousand of a number by counting the jumps to its two neighbouring marks and choosing the mark with fewer jumps.
- Out of scope: a rule for a number exactly in the middle, other places, estimating sums.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A green meadow with one long dark-brown road drawn as a number line across about 80% of the stage width. A photo cut-out of an orange carrot lies at each end and a small flag marks the halfway number. A flat-drawn grey rabbit sits on the road. Its number is written large above the road: "7,863".
- This is the tens road: carrots 7,860 and 7,870, halfway flag 7,865, and 11 small marks, one per jump. Three signposts at the top-left of the stage read "Tens", "Hundreds", "Thousands"; "Tens" is lit.
- Instruction line: "The rabbit is at 7,863. Which food is nearer? Drag the rabbit to it."
- The child is invited to drag the rabbit.
2. Scene and Objects
- Under the rabbit a tag shows its number; under each carrot a space is kept for its jump count. On the hundreds road the marks are 10 apart, on the thousands road 100 apart.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag the rabbit and drop it on a carrot. It hops there. The jump counts to both carrots then appear under them. Tap a signpost to change the road; a done road gets a tick.
- In Star Challenges 4 and 5 two rabbits wait in a tray and the child drags each onto a mark.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" and one big "Next" button, greyed out until the goal chip is green (in Star Challenge 3 it reads "Check" first). A wrong drop sends the rabbit back at once and the counts stay on show, so the child can try again.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "The rabbit is at 7,863. Which food is nearer? Drag the rabbit to it." Goal chip: "Nearest ten". Tens road, carrots 7,860 and 7,870. Guess: the drop is the guess. Result: the rabbit hops 3 jumps to 7,860. Why: "7,863 − 7,860 = 3 jumps and 7,870 − 7,863 = 7 jumps. 3 is less than 7, so 7,860 is the nearest ten." Help: guided, the 11 marks and the halfway flag are shown.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "The rabbit is at 4,618. Which food is nearer? Drag the rabbit to it." Goal chip: "Nearest hundred". Hundreds road, carrots 4,600 and 4,700, flag 4,650, marks 10 apart. Result: 18 jumps to 4,600. Why: "4,618 − 4,600 = 18 jumps and 4,700 − 4,618 = 82 jumps. 18 is less than 82, so 4,600 is the nearest hundred." Help: guided, marks and flag shown.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "The rabbit is at 8,327. Find its nearest ten, hundred and thousand." Goal chip: "Three roads". The child visits the three roads in any order and drops the rabbit on the nearer carrot of each. Tens: 8,320 and 8,330, nearest 8,330 (3 jumps). Hundreds: 8,300 and 8,400, nearest 8,300 (27 jumps). Thousands: 8,000 and 9,000, nearest 8,000 (327 jumps). Guess: the drop. Why: "8,330 − 8,327 = 3, 8,327 − 8,300 = 27 and 8,327 − 8,000 = 327. The nearest mark can be above the number or below it." Help: independent, no marks.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Two rabbits, one road. Will both go to the same food?" Goal chip: "Same carrot". Tens road 6,290 to 6,310, carrots 6,290, 6,300 and 6,310, rabbits at 6,298 and 6,303. Guess: the child taps "Yes" or "No", then drags each rabbit to its nearer carrot. Result: both hop to 6,300. Why: "6,300 − 6,298 = 2 jumps and 6,303 − 6,300 = 3 jumps, so 6,300 is the nearest ten of both." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "A rabbit is hungry. The rabbit is at 2,346. Its food has been kept at its neighbouring tens, 2,340 and 2,350. On which tens should the rabbit go to get its food, with the least number of steps?" Goal chip: "Rabbit at 2,346". The same rabbit then visits the hundreds road (2,300 and 2,400, flag 2,350): "Which of the two hundreds should the rabbit go to?", and the thousands road (2,000 and 3,000, flag 2,500): "Which number should the rabbit go to?" After each hop a sentence appears: "___ is the nearest ten (hundred, thousand) of 2,346. It will need ___ jumps to reach ___." The child drags number chips into the blanks: the two carrots and the two jump counts. Guess: the drop. Results: 2,350 with 4 jumps; 2,300 with 46 jumps; 2,000 with 346 jumps. Why: "2,350 − 2,346 = 4 jumps and 2,346 − 2,340 = 6; 2,346 − 2,300 = 46 and 2,400 − 2,346 = 54; 2,346 − 2,000 = 346 and 3,000 − 2,346 = 654." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "Fill in the boxes appropriately. Find the nearest tens, nearest hundreds and nearest thousands of 3,176, 4,017, 5,789 and 8,203." Goal chip: "Table: 0 of 12". A table of 4 rows and 3 columns. Each empty box offers two chips, the two neighbouring marks of that number, for example 3,170 or 3,180 for the tens of 3,176. Guess: tapping a chip. Results: 3,176: 3,180; 3,200; 3,000. 4,017: 4,020; 4,000; 4,000. 5,789: 5,790; 5,800; 6,000. 8,203: 8,200; 8,200; 8,000. After a tap, the jumps to both chips show in small type. Why for the tens of 3,176: "3,176 − 3,170 = 6 jumps and 3,180 − 3,176 = 4 jumps, so 3,180." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "Vijay rounded off a number to the nearest hundred. Suma rounded off the same number to the nearest thousand. Both got the same result. Circle the numbers they might have used." Goal chip: "Circle 2". Four bubbles: 7,126, 7,835, 7,030, 6,999. Guess: the child circles the bubbles they think fit and presses Check; each bubble then shows its nearest hundred and thousand with the jumps. Result: 7,030 and 6,999 turn green. Why: "7,030 and 6,999 both give 7,000 for the hundred and for the thousand. 7,126 gives 7,100 and 7,000, and 7,835 gives 7,800 and 8,000." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4. Goal line: "Think and write two numbers that have the same (a) Nearest ten. (b) Nearest hundred. (c) Nearest thousand. For example, 19 and 21 have the same nearest ten, that is, 20." Goal chip: "Same nearest: 0 of 3". Part (a): tens road 3,130 to 3,150 with carrots 3,130, 3,140, 3,150, marks 1 apart. Part (b): hundreds road 4,400 to 4,600 with carrots 4,400, 4,500, 4,600, marks 10 apart. Part (c): thousands road 5,000 to 7,000 with carrots 5,000, 6,000, 7,000, marks 100 apart. Guess: the child taps the carrot both rabbits will go to, then drops two rabbits on two different marks. Result: both hop to that carrot. Why for the pair 3,138 and 3,142: "3,140 − 3,138 = 2 jumps and 3,142 − 3,140 = 2 jumps, and the other tens are 8 jumps away." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 5. Goal line: "Think and write the numbers that have the same (a) Nearest ten and nearest hundred. (b) Nearest hundred and nearest thousand. (c) Nearest ten, hundred and thousand." Goal chip: "Same nearest: 0 of 3". Part (a): tens road 5,290 to 5,310. Part (b): hundreds road 7,900 to 8,100, marks 10 apart. Part (c): tens road 3,990 to 4,010. Guess: the child taps the carrot both rabbits will go to. The tool compares both rabbits on every road involved. Result: for example 5,297 and 5,302 share 5,300 as the nearest ten and nearest hundred. Why: "5,300 − 5,297 = 3 jumps and 5,302 − 5,300 = 2 jumps; the other tens are 7 and 8 jumps away." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- The child finds the two neighbouring marks, counts the jumps to each and sees that the mark with fewer jumps is the nearest. On three roads the nearest mark can be above on one and below on another. The child says: "Count the jumps to both marks. The nearer mark has fewer jumps."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the carrot with fewer jumps glows green, the rabbit hops one jump at a time with a gentle count, the sentence fills in, the goal chip turns green with a bounce and the strip says "Nearest found!"
- Mistake: picks the carrot with more jumps -> red strip, small shake, "This carrot needs more jumps. Which carrot needs fewer?" Both counts stay on show and the smaller one pulses.
- Mistake: picks the carrot that looks like the number (8,320 for 8,327) -> "8,320 looks like 8,327, but count the jumps: it needs 7. The other food needs 3."
- Mistake: always goes up or always goes down -> "The nearest mark can be above or below the rabbit. Count the jumps."
- Mistake: a rabbit dropped nearer to another carrot in Star Challenges 4 and 5 -> "This rabbit is nearer to another carrot. Move it closer to the one you chose." Both rabbits show their jumps.
- Hints: (1) "Which two foods are at the ends of the road? Which one looks closer?" (2) The jump counts to both carrots appear and the halfway flag glows. (3) The nearer carrot glows: "Take the rabbit to the carrot that needs fewer jumps."
- Edge cases: no card puts the rabbit on the halfway number. A rabbit dropped on a halfway mark in Star Challenges 4 and 5 hears "This spot is the same distance from both carrots. Move the rabbit a little to one side." The two rabbits must stand on different marks.
7. Ending
- Activities are done when the rabbit reaches the nearer carrot. Star Challenge 1 is done with all three sentences right, 2 with all 12 boxes right, 3 with 7,030 and 6,999, and 4 and 5 when the two rabbits in each part share the same nearest marks.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Find the two neighbouring marks of the number." "Count the jumps to each mark. The nearer mark has fewer jumps." "The nearest mark can be below or above the number." Think and talk: "Can the nearest ten of a number be above it while its nearest hundred is below it? Find a number." Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: green meadow; dark-brown road number line with marks (code-drawn); orange carrot cut-outs; flat-drawn grey rabbit; halfway flag; three signposts. English only.

media.title: The rabbit and the nearest ten
media.context: Starting point is the chapter's picture of the rabbit between two carrots at neighbouring tens, with the halfway mark. The numbers are the plan's own from the concept's worked example: rabbit at 4,197, neighbours 4,190 and 4,200, halfway mark 4,195, 3 jumps and 7 jumps. 5. Rule: two numbers have the same nearest number when both are nearer to the same food on that line.

content.text:
Worked example: (a) Write two numbers that have the same nearest hundred. (b) Write two numbers that have the same nearest ten, nearest hundred and nearest thousand.
1. (a) Pick the hundred 5,400 and take one number below it and one above it: 5,380 and 5,420.
2. 5,380 needs 5,400 − 5,380 = 20 jumps to 5,400 and 5,380 − 5,300 = 80 jumps to 5,300. 5,420 needs 5,420 − 5,400 = 20 jumps to 5,400 and 5,500 − 5,420 = 80 jumps to 5,500. Both have the nearest hundred 5,400.
3. (b) Pick the thousand 8,000 and take two numbers very close to it: 7,997 and 8,002.
4. Nearest ten: 7,997 needs 3 jumps to 8,000 and 7,997 − 7,990 = 7 jumps to 7,990. 8,002 needs 2 jumps to 8,000 and 8,010 − 8,002 = 8 jumps to 8,010. Both give 8,000.
5. Nearest hundred: 7,997 needs 3 jumps to 8,000 and 7,997 − 7,900 = 97 jumps to 7,900. 8,002 needs 2 jumps to 8,000 and 8,100 − 8,002 = 98 jumps to 8,100. Both give 8,000.
6. Nearest thousand: 7,997 needs 3 jumps to 8,000 and 7,997 − 7,000 = 997 jumps to 7,000. 8,002 needs 2 jumps to 8,000 and 9,000 − 8,002 = 998 jumps to 9,000. Both give 8,000.
Answer: (a) 5,380 and 5,420, nearest hundred 5,400. (b) 7,997 and 8,002, nearest ten, nearest hundred and nearest thousand all 8,000.

$7,126$: $26$ jumps to $7,100$ and $74$ jumps to $7,200$, so $7,100$. $126$ jumps to $7,000$ and $874$ jumps to $8,000$, so $7,000$. The results are different.
$7,835$: $35$ jumps to $7,800$ and $65$ jumps to $7,900$, so $7,800$. $835$ jumps to $7,000$ and $165$ jumps to $8,000$, so $8,000$. The results are different.
$7,030$: $30$ jumps to $7,000$ and $70$ jumps to $7,100$, so $7,000$. $30$ jumps to $7,000$ and $970$ jumps to $8,000$, so $7,000$. The results are the same.
$6,999$: $99$ jumps to $6,900$ and $1$ jump to $7,000$, so $7,000$. $999$ jumps to $6,000$ and $1$ jump to $7,000$, so $7,000$. The results are the same.
Check: $7,030$ is $30$ above $7,000$ and $6,999$ is $1$ below $7,000$, so both stand right next to $7,000$.

content.text:
1. $(a)$: Pick the ten $3,140$. $3,138$ is $2$ jumps below it and $3,142$ is $2$ jumps above it.
2. The other tens are far: $3,138 - 3,130 = 8$ jumps and $3,150 - 3,142 = 8$ jumps. Both have the nearest ten $3,140$.
3. $(b)$: Pick the hundred $4,500$. $4,480$ is $20$ jumps below it and $4,520$ is $20$ jumps above it.
4. The other hundreds are far: $4,480 - 4,400 = 80$ jumps and $4,600 - 4,520 = 80$ jumps. Both have the nearest hundred $4,500$.
5. $(c)$: Pick the thousand $6,000$. $5,900$ is $100$ jumps below it and $6,200$ is $200$ jumps above it.
[Image: Let Us Think: Ans2: solution]
6. The other thousands are far: $5,900 - 5,000 = 900$ jumps and $7,000 - 6,200 = 800$ jumps. Both have the nearest thousand $6,000$.
7. Check: $3,138$ and $3,142$ are both $2$ from $3,140$, $4,480$ and $4,520$ are both $20$ from $4,500$, and $5,900$ and $6,200$ are much nearer to $6,000$ than to $5,000$ or $7,000$.
Answer: Sample answer: $(a)$: $3,138$ and $3,142$; $(b)$: $4,480$ and $4,520$; $(c)$: $5,900$ and $6,200$. Your answer may differ.
[Image: Let Us Think: Ans2: solution (continued)]

content.text:
1. $(a)$: Pick the hundred $5,300$ and numbers right next to it: $5,297$ is $3$ jumps below it and $5,302$ is $2$ jumps above it.
2. Their nearest ten is also $5,300$: $5,297$ is $7$ jumps from $5,290$ and $5,302$ is $8$ jumps from $5,310$. Both give $5,300$ for the ten and for the hundred.
3. $(b)$: Pick the thousand $8,000$. $7,970$ is $30$ jumps below it and $8,030$ is $30$ jumps above it. The other thousands are $970$ jumps away, so both give $8,000$.
4. Their nearest hundred is also $8,000$: $7,970$ is $70$ jumps from $7,900$ and $8,030$ is $70$ jumps from $8,100$.
[Image: Let Us Think: Ans3: solution]
5. $(c)$: Pick $4,000$ and numbers very close to it: $3,998$ is $2$ jumps below it and $4,003$ is $3$ jumps above it.
6. The other tens are $3,998 - 3,990 = 8$ and $4,010 - 4,003 = 7$ jumps away. The other hundreds are $3,998 - 3,900 = 98$ and $4,100 - 4,003 = 97$ jumps away. The other thousands are $3,998 - 3,000 = 998$ and $5,000 - 4,003 = 997$ jumps away.
7. So $3,998$ and $4,003$ both have the nearest ten, hundred and thousand $4,000$.
8. Check: $5,297$ and $5,302$ are within $3$ of $5,300$, $7,970$ and $8,030$ are $30$ from $8,000$, and $3,998$ and $4,003$ are within $3$ of $4,000$, far less than the jumps to the other marks.
Answer: Sample answer: $(a)$: $5,297$ and $5,302$; $(b)$: $7,970$ and $8,030$; $(c)$: $3,998$ and $4,003$. Your answer may differ.
[Image: Let Us Think: Ans3: solution (continued)]

Their nearest hundred is also 8,000: 7,970 is 70 jumps from 7,900 and 8,030 is 70 jumps from 8,100.

media.title: Transport Explorer

tool_config.idea: Read the book's own numbers for travel and use them: how far a means of travel goes in one hour (from 3 to 5 km on foot to at least 28,000 km by spacecraft), how many digits that distance has, how far it goes in several hours (the distance in one hour times the hours), and how many vehicles a group needs (the people divided by the people one vehicle carries).
tool_config.title: Transport Explorer
tool_config.screen: One clean, warm, colourful route map in a polished educational-game look: a 3D isometric landscape with soft shadows, clear shapes and gentle animation, where a winding route runs from a Start flag to a Finish flag across fields, a river bank and a sea shore. Nothing else is drawn: no crowds, no shops, no decoration off the route. The largest element is the distance card in the middle of the screen, with its numbers in very large type. A row of eight large vehicle buttons runs along the bottom, each with a picture and a name: Foot, Horseback, Cycle, Motorbike, Train, Ship, Aircraft, Spacecraft. Every control and read-out: (1) the eight vehicle buttons, one selected at a time; choosing one moves that vehicle a short way along the route. (2) The distance card, for example 'In 1 hour: 40 to 60 km', and for the spacecraft 'In 1 hour: at least 28,000 km'. (3) Digit chips under the card, one for each number on it, such as '2 digits', with the digits coloured by place. (4) An Hours stepper with minus and plus buttons from 1 to 4 hours and a Go button: the vehicle hops along the route once for each hour, every hop the same length, and a working line shows each end of the range times the hours, for example '10 × 3 = 30'. The label 'same distance every hour (practice)' sits beside it. The Hours stepper is greyed out for the spacecraft because the book gives only a minimum. (5) A group panel: a crowd drawn in groups of ten, a 'People' read-out, the 'People in one vehicle' read-out taken from the book's list (bicycle 2, autorickshaw 3, car 4, big car 6, tempo traveller 10, boat 20, minibus 25, aeroplane 180), a Load button that fills one vehicle at a time, a 'Vehicles used' counter and a 'People left' counter. (6) An answer box that opens on a challenge card, with a Check button. (7) Hint, Undo and Reset buttons, a progress strip of dots with one dot for each card, Back and Next buttons in the same bottom corners on every card, and a Restart button. Only the controls the current card needs are shown.
feedback: A right answer turns the card green with a tick, and the vehicle drives to the Finish flag. The working appears in one line, for example 10 × 3 = 30.
A distance that is not in the chosen range shows the range beside it and says whether the distance is less than the first number or more than the last number.
A wrong number of digits lights up the digits of the number one by one and counts them aloud.
A wrong number of hours or vehicles shows the hops or the loaded vehicles on the route and the people still left, so the student sees what is missing.
Each hour of the journey stays on the route as a hop of the same length, so the total is seen being built.
tool_config.done_when: Every card is done and the student has opened at least five of the eight vehicle cards.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1 (read): Tap Foot, then Spacecraft. How many digits does the number on each card have? Answer: foot, 3 to 5 km, 1 digit; spacecraft, at least 28,000 km, 5 digits.

Card 2 (find the means): Practice value: a traveller covers 30 km in one hour. Tap the vehicles and find the one whose card holds 30. Answer: the ship, 25 to 45 km, because 25 is less than 30 and 30 is less than 45; every other card misses 30.
Card 3 (hours): Pick Horseback and set 3 hours. Fill in both ends of the range for 3 hours, with the same distance every hour (practice). Answer: 10 × 3 = 30 and 15 × 3 = 45, so 30 to 45 km.

Card 4 (vehicles): Practice value: a group of 120 people. Load them into boats (20 each) and then into tempo travellers (10 each). How many of each, and which needs fewer? Answer: 120 ÷ 20 = 6 boats and 120 ÷ 10 = 12 tempo travellers; the boat carries more people, so fewer boats are needed.
Card 5 (the book's question): A cyclist can cover 15 km in one hour. How much distance will she cover in 4 hours, if she maintains the same speed? Answer: 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 60, so 15 × 4 = 60 km.

Card 6 (the book's question): A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them to go on a trip using the following modes of travel? The numbers in the bracket indicate the number of people that can travel in one vehicle. (a) Bicycle (2) (b) Autorickshaw (3) (c) Car (4) (d) Big car (6) (e) Tempo traveller (10) (f) Boat (20) (g) Minibus (25) (h) Aeroplane (180). Answer: 461 + 439 = 900 people; 450, 300, 225, 150, 90, 45, 36 and 5 vehicles.

hint_ladder.text: Which card is open, and what does it show: a range or a minimum?
For many hours, take the distance in one hour as many times as the number of hours. For vehicles, divide the people by the people in one vehicle.
A distance fits a range when it is at least the first number and at most the last number. To check vehicles, multiply the vehicles by the people in one.
Worked step: horseback, 10 to 15 km, 2 hours: 10 × 2 = 20 and 15 × 2 = 30, so 20 to 30 km. For the cyclist and the school the same step is shown with their own numbers, then a similar card follows.

media.instructions_for_student: The student finds the distance in several hours by repeating the distance of one hour, and the vehicles for a group by dividing the people by the people in one vehicle.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Transport Explorer
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S22.T22.C92.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: We the Travellers - I, Travelling, Now and Then and Let Us Do (travelling) Questions 1 and 2: the cyclist who covers 15 km in one hour (4 hours), and the school of 461 girls and 439 boys with vehicles of 2, 3, 4, 6, 10, 20, 25 and 180 people (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student finds the distance in several hours by taking the distance of one hour once for every hour, and finds the vehicles for a group by dividing the people by the people in one vehicle.
- Out of scope: the list of distances for each means of travel, counting digits, speed units, division with a remainder.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A country route drawn as a flat illustration, straightened across the stage: a Start flag on the left, green fields, a river bank and a Finish flag. Along it runs a ruler with milestone posts. A photo cut-out of a rider on a horse stands at Start, about 12% of the stage width.
- A round clock button "+1 hour" sits at the bottom-left of the stage. At the top-right is a distance box "Distance: 0 km" and a chip "Hours: 0".
- Instruction line: "A rider covers 14 km in 1 hour. How far in 3 hours? Make a guess."
- Three guess chips lie under the ruler: "28 km", "42 km", "56 km". The child is invited to tap one.
2. Scene and Objects
- Route view (Activities 1 to 3 and Star Challenge 1): ruler with a milestone post at every hop, a vehicle cut-out (horse rider, motorbike, ship, cycle), the clock button, the distance box and an answer dial of digit spinners (hundreds, tens, ones) where the answer needs one.
- Loading view (Activities 4 to 6 and Star Challenges 2 and 3): on the left a crowd drawn as a block of small flat people with its number written large, for example "People: 80"; in the middle a row of vehicle cut-outs (tempo traveller, boat, minibus, bicycle, autorickshaw, car, big car, aeroplane), each with its size written under it, "Tempo traveller (10)"; on the right two counters, "Vehicles used" and "People left". The row shows up to 10 vehicles, then "+ more".
3. Main Interaction
- Route view: tap the clock button once for each hour; the vehicle hops one equal hop along the ruler and the distance box adds one hop. Loading view: tap the round "+" to load one more vehicle; each loaded vehicle takes its full number of people from the crowd. "−" removes one. The dial: tap above a spinner to go up and below it to go down.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" and one big button. In Activities 1, 2, 4 and 5 it reads "Next" from the start and is greyed out until the hops or the loading are done; in the other pills it reads "Check" and becomes "Next" when the answer is right. "Reset" returns the hops or the loading to the start. A wrong answer changes nothing on the stage.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "A rider covers 14 km in 1 hour. How far in 3 hours? Make a guess." Goal chip: "Hops of 14 km". Guess: the child taps "28 km", "42 km" or "56 km" and then taps the clock 3 times. Result: hops reach 14, 28, 42 and the chosen chip turns green if it is 42 km. Why: "14 + 14 + 14 = 42, so 3 × 14 = 42 km." Help: guided, each hop is labelled with its distance.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "A motorbike covers 48 km in 1 hour. How far in 5 hours?" Goal chip: "Hops of 48 km". Guess chips: "53 km", "144 km", "240 km". The child taps the clock 5 times. Result: 48, 96, 144, 192, 240. Why: "5 hops of 48 each: 5 × 48 = 240 km." Help: guided, hop labels shown.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "A ship covers 35 km in 1 hour. How far in 6 hours?" Goal chip: "Hops of 35 km". Guess: the child sets the dial to the distance and presses Check. Result: the ship hops 6 times to 210 km. Why: "6 hops of 35 each: 6 × 35 = 210 km." Help: independent, no hop labels.
- Activity 4 (guided). Goal line: "80 people go in tempo travellers. Each carries 10 people. How many tempo travellers?" Goal chip: "Vehicles: 0 of 1". Loading view. Guess: the child taps "7", "8" or "10" and then loads vehicles with "+". Result: after 8 vehicles "People left" is 0. Why: "80 ÷ 10 = 8, and 8 × 10 = 80." Help: guided, both counters shown.
- Activity 5 (guided). Goal line: "The same 80 people go in boats. Each boat carries 20 people. Will you need more, the same or fewer vehicles?" Goal chip: "Vehicles: 0 of 1". Guess: the child taps "More", "The same" or "Fewer", then loads boats. Result: 4 boats. Why: "80 ÷ 20 = 4, and 4 × 20 = 80. A boat carries more people, so fewer vehicles are needed." Help: guided.
- Activity 6 (independent). Goal line: "200 people go in minibuses. Each carries 25 people. How many minibuses?" Goal chip: "Vehicles: 0 of 1". Guess: the child sets the dial and presses Check. Result: 8 minibuses load and "People left" shows 0. Why: "200 ÷ 25 = 8, and 8 × 25 = 200." Help: independent, counters hidden until Check.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "A cyclist can cover 15 km in one hour. How much distance will she cover in 4 hours, if she maintains the same speed?" Goal chip: "Distance in 4 hours". Guess: the child sets the dial and presses Check. Result: the cyclist hops 4 times: 15, 30, 45, 60. Why: "15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 60, so 4 × 15 = 60 km." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them to go on a trip using the following modes of travel? The numbers in the bracket indicate the number of people that can travel in one vehicle. (a) Bicycle (2) (b) Autorickshaw (3) (c) Car (4) (d) Big car (6)". Goal chip: "Vehicles: 0 of 4". First two crowd blocks, "461 girls" and "439 boys", are shown; the child taps the total of the school: "890", "900" or "910", and the blocks merge into one crowd of 900. Then for each vehicle the child sets the dial and presses Check. Guess: the dial. Results: 450, 300, 225, 150. Why: "461 + 439 = 900 people. 900 ÷ 2 = 450, 900 ÷ 3 = 300, 900 ÷ 4 = 225 and 900 ÷ 6 = 150." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them to go on a trip using the following modes of travel? (e) Tempo traveller (10) (f) Boat (20) (g) Minibus (25) (h) Aeroplane (180)". Goal chip: "Vehicles: 0 of 4". The crowd of 900 is shown. Guess: the dial, as before. Results: 90, 45, 36, 5. Why: "900 ÷ 10 = 90, 900 ÷ 20 = 45, 900 ÷ 25 = 36 and 900 ÷ 180 = 5." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Each hour is one more equal hop, so the distance in many hours is the distance in one hour taken once for every hour. Each vehicle takes the same number of people, so the vehicles needed are the people divided by the people in one vehicle, and multiplying back checks it. The child says: "Distance in many hours is the distance in one hour times the hours. Vehicles needed are the people divided by the people in one vehicle."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the answer box turns green, the vehicle hops or the vehicles load one by one with a running count, the goal chip bounces and the strip says "Spot on!"
- Mistake: adds the distance and the hours (53 km in Activity 2) -> red strip, small shake, "48 + 5 mixes up the distance and the hours. Take 48 km once for each of the 5 hours." The clock button pulses.
- Mistake: the wrong number of hops (175 km in Activity 3) -> "That is 5 hops of 35 km. There are 6 hours, so we need 6 hops." The hours chip pulses.
- Mistake: too few vehicles -> "225 bicycles carry only 450 people. We need to carry 900. Try more." The tool uses the child's number and the vehicle size in this line.
- Mistake: too many vehicles -> "Your vehicles can carry more people than we have. Try fewer."
- Mistake: multiplies instead of dividing, or thinks a bigger vehicle needs more vehicles -> "A vehicle that carries more people means fewer vehicles are needed." The vehicle size label pulses.
- Mistake: wrong total in Star Challenge 2 -> "Add ones, tens and hundreds. 1 + 9 = 10 ones make 1 ten." The crowd blocks pulse.
- Hints: (1) "How far does one hour take you? How many people does one vehicle take?" (2) The first two hops play with their counter, or the first two vehicles load. (3) The working is shown with one hop or one vehicle left for the child to finish.
- Edge cases: every number here divides exactly, so there is never a remainder. A dial of 000 shows "Set the dial first".
7. Ending
- Activities are done when the answer is right. Star Challenge 1 is done with 60 km, Star Challenge 2 with 450, 300, 225 and 150 vehicles, and Star Challenge 3 with 90, 45, 36 and 5 vehicles.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "The distance in many hours is the distance in one hour times the hours." "The vehicles needed are the people divided by the people in one vehicle." "A vehicle that carries more people means fewer vehicles are needed." Think and talk: "A boat carries 20 people and a minibus carries 25 people. Which will you need fewer of? Why?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: flat country route with flags, fields and a river bank; ruler with milestone posts (code-drawn); photo cut-outs of a rider on a horse, a motorbike, a ship, a cycle, a bicycle, an autorickshaw, a car, a big car, a tempo traveller, a boat, a minibus and an aeroplane; flat drawn crowd; round clock button. English only.

For now we use kilometres, and 1 km = 1,000 m. Rule: a distance fits a means of travel when it is at least the first number and at most the last number of its range. 1. A means fits when 50 is at least its first number and at most its last number. 2. On foot (3 to 5), on horseback (10 to 15), by cycle (12 to 20) and by ship (25 to 45): 50 is more than the last number each time, so none fits. 3. By aircraft (750 to 920) and by spacecraft (minimum 28,000): 50 is less than the first number, so neither fits. 4. By motorbike (40 to 60): 40 is less than 50 and 50 is less than 60, so it fits. 5. By train (40 to 160): 40 is less than 50 and 50 is less than 160, so it fits. 6. 50 has 2 digits. Answer: A motorbike or a train; 50 is a 2-digit number

topics.summary: People travelled on foot, on animals and in boats long ago, and now they use cycles, cars, trains, ships, aeroplanes and spacecraft. The book gives how far a person generally travels in one hour, from a 1-digit number to a 5-digit number of kilometres. The distance in many hours is the distance in one hour times the number of hours, and the vehicles needed for a group are the people divided by the people in one vehicle.

content.text:
We learnt that people in the past travelled on foot, on animals, and used boats and sailing ships. The animals that have been used for travelling include bullocks, horses, donkeys, mules, and elephants. In hilly and snow-covered regions, yaks, dogs, and reindeers have been used, while camels have been used in deserts.
Now, people use bicycles, motorbikes, cars, buses, trains, ships, and aeroplanes to travel from one place to another. Submarines are used to go deep under water. Humans are also using spacecraft to travel to outer space.

Worked example: Mira makes a travel card for four places. Which means of travel from the book fits each place? (a) crossing water in the past, (b) a desert, (c) deep under water, (d) outer space.
1. (a) Crossing water in the past: people used boats and sailing ships.
2. (b) A desert: camels have been used in deserts.
3. (c) Deep under water: submarines are used to go deep under water.
4. (d) Outer space: humans use spacecraft to travel to outer space.
5. Check: each answer names a place from the book and its own means of travel.
Answer: (a) boats and sailing ships, (b) camels, (c) submarines, (d) spacecraft

content.text:
In an hour a person can generally travel
(a) 3 to 5 km on foot.
(b) 10 to 15 km on horseback.
(c) 12 to 20 km by cycle.
(d) 40 to 60 km by motorbike.
(e) 40 to 160 km by train.
(f) 25 to 45 km by ship.
(g) 750 to 920 km by aircraft.
(h) minimum 28,000 km by spacecraft.
Usually, we measure distances in sea and air using nautical miles. For now, we will use 1 km = 1,000 m. By now, you know different units of measuring length. We will study the units for measuring length, kilometre, in detail in a later chapter.

content.text:
1. Predict first: in one hour, how far can a person go on foot, and how far in a spacecraft? Guess one number for each.
2. The book says a person can generally travel 3 to 5 km on foot, 10 to 15 km on horseback, 12 to 20 km by cycle and 40 to 60 km by motorbike in an hour.
3. By train 40 to 160 km, by ship 25 to 45 km and by aircraft 750 to 920 km. By spacecraft the minimum is 28,000 km.
4. So the distance in an hour runs from a 1-digit number, 3 km on foot, to a 5-digit number, 28,000 km by spacecraft.
5. At sea and in the air, distances are usually measured in nautical miles. For now we use kilometres, and 1 km = 1,000 m.
6. Rule: a distance fits a means of travel when it is at least the first number and at most the last number of its range.

content.text:
Worked example: Suppose a traveller covers 50 km in one hour. Which means of travel in the book's list can do that, and how many digits does 50 have?
1. A means fits when 50 is at least its first number and at most its last number.
2. On foot (3 to 5), on horseback (10 to 15), by cycle (12 to 20) and by ship (25 to 45): 50 is more than the last number each time, so none fits.
3. By aircraft (750 to 920) and by spacecraft (minimum 28,000): 50 is less than the first number, so neither fits.
4. By motorbike (40 to 60): 40 is less than 50 and 50 is less than 60, so it fits.
5. By train (40 to 160): 40 is less than 50 and 50 is less than 160, so it fits.
6. 50 has 2 digits.
Answer: A motorbike or a train; 50 is a 2-digit number

content.text:
1. Predict first: 12 children go on a trip in cars that carry 4 children each. How many cars do they need, 3, 4 or 8?
2. Each car takes 4 children. Count in 4s: 4, 8, 12. That is 3 cars, and 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
3. The number of vehicles is the number of people divided by the number of people in one vehicle.
4. A vehicle that carries more people needs fewer vehicles. The same 12 children need 3 cars of 4, but only 2 big cars of 6, because 12 ÷ 6 = 2.
5. Check by multiplying: 3 × 4 = 12 and 2 × 6 = 12.
6. Rule: divide the people by the number one vehicle carries, then check by multiplying.

content.text:
Worked example: A group of 120 people goes on a trip. How many vehicles are needed if each car carries 4 people? How many if each big car carries 6 people?
1. People in the group: 120. People in one car: 4.
2. Cars needed: 120 ÷ 4 = 30.
3. Check: 30 × 4 = 120, so 30 cars carry all 120 people.
4. People in one big car: 6. Big cars needed: 120 ÷ 6 = 20.
5. Check: 20 × 6 = 120, so 20 big cars carry all 120 people.
6. A big car carries more people, so fewer vehicles are needed.
Answer: 30 cars, or 20 big cars

content.text: A cyclist can cover $15\text{ km}$ in one hour. How much distance will she cover in $4$ hours, if she maintains the same speed?

content.book_number: Let Us Do (travelling), Q1 cyclist
content.question_tex: A cyclist can cover $15\text{ km}$ in one hour. How much distance will she cover in $4$ hours, if she maintains the same speed?
content.publication_text: A cyclist can cover $15\text{ km}$ in one hour. How much distance will she cover in $4$ hours, if she maintains the same speed?

content.text:
1. In $1$ hour the cyclist covers $15\text{ km}$.
2. In $2$ hours: $15 + 15 = 30\text{ km}$.
3. In $3$ hours: $30 + 15 = 45\text{ km}$.
4. In $4$ hours: $45 + 15 = 60\text{ km}$.
5. Check by multiplying: $15 \times 4 = 60\text{ km}$.
Answer: $60\text{ km}$

content.text:

4. $(b)$: Autorickshaw: $900 \div 3 = 300$.
5. $(c)$: Car: $900 \div 4 = 225$.
6. $(d)$: Big car: $900 \div 6 = 150$.

topics.summary: Large numbers are not only about travel. When we count one small part and multiply by the number of parts, we can find a big count without counting one by one, and then say how many digits it has.

content.text:
We saw that the distance (in kilometre) covered by different means of transport in an hour can range from a 1-digit number to a 5-digit number. Can we find other contexts around us that contain numbers in this range? Let us consider the situation below.
Now, let us try this with our school.
(a) Our school has ________ classrooms.
(b) There are ________ students in my class.
(c) Our classroom has ________ books in total.

4. Now try it with your school: our school has ___ classrooms, there are ___ students in my class, and our classroom has ___ books in total. Say how many digits each count has.
5. Rule: count one small part, multiply by the number of parts, then count the digits.

content.text:
Worked example: Suppose each sheet has 100 stickers and a box holds 40 sheets. How many stickers are in the box? Is the count a 4-digit or a 5-digit number?
1. One sheet has 100 stickers.
2. 10 sheets have 100 × 10 = 1,000 stickers.
3. 40 sheets are 4 groups of 10 sheets: 4 × 1,000 = 4,000 stickers.
4. Check: 100 × 40 = 4,000.
5. 4,000 has 4 digits, so the count is a 4-digit number.
Answer: 4,000 stickers, a 4-digit number

concepts.concept_name: Finding Large Numbers Around Us: Q1

content.text:
1. Pick a thing to count: the words in one chapter of the maths book.
2. Estimate one part: a page has about $150$ words.
3. Count the parts: the chapter has about $16$ pages.
4. $10$ pages have $10 \times 150 = 1,500$ words.
5. $6$ pages have $6 \times 150 = 900$ words.
6. Add the parts: $1,500 + 900 = 2,400$ words.
7. Check: $2,400$ has $4$ digits, so it is a $4$-digit number.
Answer: Sample answer: the words in one chapter, about $2,400$, a $4$-digit number: $16$ pages with about $150$ words each. Your answer may differ.

concepts.concept_name: Finding Large Numbers Around Us: Q2

content.text:
1. (i): Count the pages in one notebook from each child. Suppose the class has $40$ children and a notebook has about $100$ pages.
2. $10$ notebooks have $10 \times 100 = 1,000$ pages.
3. $40$ notebooks are $4$ groups of $10$: $4 \times 1,000 = 4,000$ pages, a $4$-digit number.
4. (ii): Count all the notebooks. Suppose each child has $5$ notebooks: $40 \times 5 = 200$ notebooks.
5. $200$ notebooks with about $100$ pages each: $200 \times 100 = 20,000$ pages, a $5$-digit number.
6. Check the digits: $4,000$ has $4$ digits and $20,000$ has $5$ digits.
Answer: Sample answer: (i): pages in $40$ notebooks, about $4,000$, a $4$-digit number; (ii): pages in $200$ notebooks, about $20,000$, a $5$-digit number. Your answer may differ.

media.title: Puzzle Lab

tool_config.idea: Play the book's three pastime puzzles with their exact rules and find the thinking that wins each one: the safe pairs in the river, the equal piles in the pebbles game, and the table of 9 in Mira's digits.
tool_config.title: Puzzle Lab
tool_config.screen: A warm, colourful, polished educational-game scene: a compact hub on a small isometric table inside a train compartment, with three large door cards, River Crossing, Pile of Pebbles and Fun Puzzle (digits), soft shadows, gentle animation and no clutter. One door opens one scene at a time, and the puzzle board is always the largest thing on screen. River Crossing: a river with a near bank and a far bank, a boat for the boatman and one thing, and a large lion, sheep and bundle of grass that the student taps to put in the boat. Controls: Cross (the boat moves), Undo, Reset. Read-outs: a trip counter (Trips), the names of who is on each bank, and a Safe or Not safe banner for the bank the boatman has just left. Pile of Pebbles: two large piles of pebbles drawn as stacks, with a pile size choice of 1, 2, 3 or 7 pebbles in each pile (1, 2 and 3 are practice games, 7 is the book's game). The student taps pebbles on one pile to choose how many to take and the chosen pebbles lift. Controls: Take, Who plays first (You or Computer), Undo, Reset. The computer partner plays any allowed move. Read-outs: Your turn or Computer's turn, and the number of pebbles in each pile. Fun Puzzle (digits): two digit slots with tiles 1 to 9, and a rule note that the two digits must be different. Controls: Make numbers (shows the two 2-digit numbers), Subtract (shows the bigger number minus the smaller number and the difference), Use these digits (feeds the two digits of the difference into the slots for the next round), Undo, Reset. Read-outs: a growing list of every round, and a stamp when one digit is left. On every scene: Hint, Back and Next in the same place, progress dots and a Restart button.
feedback: In the river scene a move that leaves the sheep with the lion or with the grass on a bank without the boatman makes the two shake and says which one eats which, then the boat goes back to where it was.
A move that tries to put two things in the boat is refused with the message that the boat takes one thing at a time.
In the pebbles scene every move is shown as the piles before and after, and the piles glow green when they are equal after the student's move.
In the digits scene each round shows the two numbers, the difference of the numbers and the difference of the digits in two different colours, and a difference in the table of 9 glows.
Two equal digits are turned back with a note that the digits must be different.
tool_config.done_when: Every card is done: the river is solved in 7 trips, a game of 7 and 7 pebbles is won, and Mira's process has been run on the digits 3 and 7 and on digits whose numbers differ by 27.

challenges: River: tick the pairs that can be left alone on a bank: lion and sheep, sheep and grass, lion and grass. Answer: only the lion and the grass.
River: make the first crossing so that nothing is eaten. Answer: take the sheep across, because the lion and the grass can stay together.
Pebbles: choose 2 pebbles in each pile and let the computer play first. Whatever the computer takes from one pile, take the same number from the other pile. Answer: you take the last pebble and win.
Digits: choose the digits 1 and 6, then press Make numbers, Subtract and Use these digits until one digit is left. Answer: 61 − 16 = 45, then 54 − 45 = 9.

River: How can the boatman take the lion, sheep, and grass across the river? Help him so that he can ferry the lion, sheep, and grass across the river safely, and in the minimum number of trips. Answer: 7 trips: take the sheep across, go back alone, take the lion across, bring the sheep back, take the grass across, go back alone, take the sheep across.

Pebbles: There are two piles of pebbles. Each pile contains 7 pebbles. Each player can pick as many pebbles they want from either of the piles. The player who picks the last pebble wins. Try this game with your friends. Now, how do you play so that you win? Answer: let the other player go first, and whatever they take from one pile, take the same number from the other pile. You take the last pebble.

Mira's puzzle: take any two different digits, make two 2-digit numbers using them, subtract the smaller number from the bigger number, then use the two digits in the difference and repeat until you get a 1-digit number. Start with the digits 3 and 7. Then find different digits such that the difference between the numbers is 27. Answer: 73 − 37 = 36, 63 − 36 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9. Digits that differ by 3 give 27, for example 1 and 4 with 41 − 14 = 27.

hint_ladder.text: What are the rules of this puzzle, and what must you find: a safe order, a winning way to play, or the number at the end?
Look for what must be true: which pairs can stay alone, what stays the same after a move, or what the differences have in common.

River: only the lion and the grass can stay alone together, so the sheep goes first. Pebbles: take the same number from the other pile as the other player took. Digits: write each difference and look at the table of 9.
The tool shows the next move itself, the sheep crossing, the copying move in the pebbles, or the next round of subtractions, and then gives a similar card.

student_does: Each door card shows one small picture and one question from the videos, which pair can be left alone on a bank, what stays the same after the second player's move, and what is common in the differences. The student taps an answer to open the door.

The student moves the lion, sheep and grass into the boat and across the river and watches the Safe or Not safe banner, plays small piles of pebbles against the computer, and runs Mira's steps on digits of their own choice while reading each difference.

The student solves each puzzle exactly as the book gives it: the river crossing with the lion, sheep and grass in the fewest trips, the two piles of 7 pebbles played so that they win, and Mira's process with the digits 3 and 7, then digits whose numbers differ by 27.

media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Puzzle Lab
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S27.T27.C112.2D1
- Tool type: Puzzle
- Textbook source: We the Travellers - I, Pastime Mathematics: river crossing, pile of pebbles (7 and 7), Mira's puzzle (digits 3 and 7) (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student solves three puzzles by thinking first: listing safe pairs, looking for what stays the same after a move, and writing every round to see what the differences share.
- Out of scope: proofs with algebra, digits above 9, the digit 0 in Mira's puzzle, other puzzles.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A river scene fills the stage: a near bank with a flat-drawn boatman, lion and sheep, a photo cut-out of a bundle of grass and a wooden boat, and a far bank on the right. A counter "Trips: 0" is at the top-right. Three pair cards sit on the near bank: "Lion + Sheep", "Sheep + Grass", "Lion + Grass", each with Safe and Not safe toggles.
- Instruction line: "Which pairs can be left alone on a bank? Tap Safe or Not safe." The child is invited to tap the first toggle.
2. Scene and Objects
- The scene changes with the pill. River: the boat takes the boatman and one thing at most. Pebbles: two piles of grey pebbles on a wooden board, sizes written large, a label "Your turn" or "Computer's turn". Digits: a notepad on a train table with two digit slots, tiles 1 to 9 (no 0, because 05 is not a 2-digit number), the steps (a), (b), (c) and a list of rounds.
3. Main Interaction
- River: tap a thing to put it in the boat (tap again to take it out), then tap "Cross"; the boat may also go back empty. Pebbles: a turn takes 1 or more pebbles from one pile only: tap a pebble to lift it and all above it, then tap "Take". Digits: drag two different tiles into the slots and tap "Go"; the digits of the difference slide into the slots for the next round.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" and one big button that reads "Cross", "Take", "Go" or "Check" and becomes "Next" when the pill is done.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Which pairs can be left alone on a bank? Tap Safe or Not safe." Goal chip: "Safe pair". Guess: the child sets the three toggles and presses Check. Result: "Lion + Sheep" and "Sheep + Grass" turn red, "Lion + Grass" turns green. Why: "Only the lion and the grass can be left alone." Then: "Make the first crossing so that nothing is eaten." Only the sheep is right. Why: "The sheep is in both unsafe pairs, so it goes first." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Play 4 and 4. The computer goes first. Take the same number from the other pile." Goal chip: "Take the last pebble". Guess: the child taps "Me" or "The computer" for who wins if you always copy. Result: the child takes the last pebble. Why: "After each of your moves the two piles were equal, for example 3 and 3, then 1 and 1, then 0 and 0." Help: guided, a mirror line sits between the piles.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "A boatman wants to cross a river in a boat. He has to take a lion, a sheep, and a bundle of grass with him. He can take one of them at a time. If the sheep and grass are left on the shore, the sheep will eat the grass. And, if the sheep and lion are left on the shore, the lion will eat the sheep. How can the boatman take the lion, sheep, and grass across the river? Help him so that he can ferry the lion, sheep, and grass across the river safely, and in the minimum number of trips." Goal chip: "Trips: 0". Guess: the child taps "5", "7" or "9" trips first. Result: all three on the far bank in 7 trips; any safe 7-trip plan is right, such as sheep, back alone, lion, sheep back, grass, back alone, sheep. More trips: "Safe, but can you use fewer trips?" Why: "4 trips to the far bank and 3 trips back: 4 + 3 = 7." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "There are two piles of pebbles. Each pile contains 7 pebbles. Each player can pick as many pebbles they want from either of the piles. The player who picks the last pebble wins. Try this game with your friends. Now, how do you play so that you win?" Goal chip: "Win the game". The child picks piles of 1, 2, 3 or 7 and who goes first. Guess: the child taps "First" or "Second" for the winning turn. Result: a won game of 7 and 7. Why: "After each of your moves the piles were equal, such as 4 and 4, 3 and 3, 0 and 0. Your friend takes from one pile only, so your friend can never empty both." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "Take any two different digits, for example 3 and 7. Make two 2-digit numbers using them. Subtract the smaller number from the bigger number. Now, use the two digits in the difference and repeat. Continue this process until you get a 1-digit number. Write the whole process." Goal chip: "Reach 1 digit". Digits 3 and 7. Guess: the child taps the end digit first. Rounds: 73 − 37 = 36, 63 − 36 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9. Why: "9 has one digit, so the process stops." Help: guided, the steps (a), (b), (c) stay shown beside the slots.
- Star Challenge 4. Goal line: "How did Mira know what the 1-digit number in the end would be? Let us explore." Goal chip: "Explore: 0 of 4". Part (1): the differences 36, 27, 45, 9 are shown; the child taps what they share: "All in the table of 9", "All even" or "All 2-digit". Part (2): the child runs another pair and taps what the differences share and the end. Part (3): the child taps three pairs that give a 1-digit number in the first step, then the pattern "The digits are next to each other". Part (4): the child taps a pair whose numbers differ by 27, such as 1 and 4. Guess: each part starts with a tap. Why: "36 = 9 × 4, 27 = 9 × 3, 45 = 9 × 5, 9 = 9 × 1 and 41 − 14 = 27." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 5. Goal line: "Extend this table by choosing appropriate digits so that the resulting differences are 2, 3, 5, and 7 respectively. What do the differences between the digits indicate?" Goal chip: "Rows: 0 of 4". For each new row the child drops two tiles whose difference is 2, 3, 5 or 7, and the tool shows the difference of the numbers, for example 1 and 3 give 31 − 13 = 18. Then the child taps the rule: "9 times the difference of the digits", "the same as the difference of the digits" or "10 times the difference of the digits". Guess: the rule is tapped first. Why: "18 = 9 × 2, 27 = 9 × 3, 45 = 9 × 5 and 63 = 9 × 7 are all in the table of 9." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 6. Goal line: "List the numbers that give a 1-digit number in the third subtraction. Identify pairs of digits that lead to the 1-digit number after the maximum possible number of subtractions." Goal chip: "Pairs: 0 of 14". A triangle of 36 tiles, one per pair of digits from 1 to 9. A tap flips a tile to show its count of subtractions and its two numbers. Part 1: the child stars the 7 pairs with count 3: 1 and 4, 1 and 9, 2 and 5, 3 and 6, 4 and 7, 5 and 8, 6 and 9. Part 2: the child stars the 7 pairs with the most subtractions, 5: 1 and 3, 2 and 4, 3 and 5, 4 and 6, 5 and 7, 6 and 8, 7 and 9. Guess: before flipping, the child taps the gap between digits (1 to 8) that needs the most subtractions. Why: "31 − 13 = 18, 81 − 18 = 63, 63 − 36 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- The safe pairs decide the river moves. Equal piles after your move leave your friend no way to take the last pebble. Every difference in Mira's puzzle is in the table of 9. The child says: "List the safe pairs first. Play a small game first."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the board glows green, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce and the strip says "You solved it!"
- Mistake: leaves the sheep with the lion or the grass -> red strip, small shake, "The lion eats the sheep if they are left alone." or "The sheep eats the grass if they are left alone." The boat rows back.
- Mistake: two things in the boat -> "The boat takes one thing at a time."
- Mistake: does not copy -> "The piles are not equal now. Take the same number from the other pile." In Activity 2 the move is undone; in Star Challenge 2 the game goes on and a lost game says "Try again and copy your friend's move."
- Mistake: two equal digits -> "The two digits must be different." Mistake: mixes the two differences -> "The digits 2 and 5 differ by 3. The numbers 52 and 25 differ by 27." Both show in two colours.
- Edge cases: the digit 0 is not offered; 9 is the only possible end.
- Hints: (1) "Which pairs can stay alone?", "Try the small game first.", "Write down every round." (2) The unsafe pairs glow red, equal piles are marked, the differences light up in a table of 9. (3) "Take the sheep first.", "Take the same number from the other pile.", the next round is filled in.
7. Ending
- Star Challenge 1 is done in 7 trips, 2 with a won game of 7 and 7, 3 when the process ends in 9, and 4, 5 and 6 when every part is right.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "List which pairs are safe to leave alone before you move." "In a big game, play a small game first and look for what stays the same." "In Mira's puzzle the differences are in the table of 9 and the end is 9." Think and talk: "Pick two digits that are 2 apart. How many subtractions do you need? Is it more than for digits that are next to each other?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: river scene; photo cut-outs of a wooden boat, a bundle of grass, grey pebbles; flat drawings of a boatman, a lion, a sheep; notepad; digit tiles 1 to 9. English only.

Subtract the smaller from the bigger: 52 − 25 = 27. 3. Use the two digits of 27, which are 2 and 7. The numbers are 27 and 72, and 72 − 27 = 45. 4. Use the two digits of 45, which are 4 and 5. The numbers are 45 and 54, and 54 − 45 = 9. 5. 9 has one digit, so we stop. The end is 9. 6. Look at the differences 27, 45 and 9. They are all in the table of 9: 27 = 9 × 3, 45 = 9 × 5 and 9 = 9 × 1. 7. The digits 2 and 5 differ by 3, because 5 − 2 = 3. The numbers 25 and 52 differ by 27. These are two different differences. content.text:
Worked example: The boatman has a lion, a sheep and a bundle of grass. Which pairs can he leave alone on a bank, and what does that tell us about his first crossing?
1. The boat takes one thing at a time, so every crossing leaves two things behind on the bank.
2. List the three pairs he could leave behind: lion and sheep, sheep and grass, lion and grass.

content.text:
Worked example: Two piles have 2 pebbles each. You play second. Write every first move your friend can make and your answer to it. Who wins, and what stays the same?
1. Start with 2 and 2. Your friend can take 2 pebbles from one pile, or take 1 pebble from one pile.
2. If your friend takes 2 from one pile, the piles are 0 and 2.
3. You take the 2 pebbles of the other pile. The piles are 0 and 0. You took the last pebble and win.
4. If your friend takes 1 from one pile, the piles are 1 and 2.
5. You take 1 from the pile of 2. The piles are 1 and 1.
6. Your friend must take 1 from a pile. The piles are 0 and 1.
7. You take the last pebble and win.
8. Look at the piles after each of your moves: 0 and 0, and 1 and 1. Both times the two piles were equal.
Answer: With 2 and 2 the player who goes second wins every game, and after each move of that player the two piles are equal

Now, it's Mira's turn. She gives a fun puzzle to Sanju with the following steps:
(a) Take any two different digits.
(b) Make two 2-digit numbers using them.
(c) Subtract the smaller number from the bigger number.
Now, use the two digits in the difference and repeat steps (b) and (c).
Continue this process until you get a 1-digit number. Even before everyone could finish, Mira exclaimed, "Mind you! No matter which two numbers you choose, you will get 9 in the end."

content.text:
1. Predict first: take the digits 2 and 5 and follow Mira's steps. What do you think you will get at the end?
2. Step (a): the digits are 2 and 5. Step (b): the numbers are 25 and 52. Step (c): 52 − 25 = 27.
3. Repeat with the digits 2 and 7: 72 − 27 = 45. Repeat with 4 and 5: 54 − 45 = 9. We stop at a 1-digit number.
4. Write every step in a row and look for what is common. The differences 27, 45 and 9 are all in the table of 9.
5. Do not mix up two differences. The digits 2 and 5 differ by 3, but the numbers 25 and 52 differ by 27.
6. Rule: when a puzzle repeats a step, write down every round and look for what stays the same.

content.text:
Worked example: Follow Mira's steps with the digits 2 and 5. What do you get at the end, and what do you notice about the differences?
1. Take the digits 2 and 5. The two 2-digit numbers are 25 and 52.
2. Subtract the smaller from the bigger: 52 − 25 = 27.
3. Use the two digits of 27, which are 2 and 7. The numbers are 27 and 72, and 72 − 27 = 45.
4. Use the two digits of 45, which are 4 and 5. The numbers are 45 and 54, and 54 − 45 = 9.
5. 9 has one digit, so we stop. The end is 9.
6. Look at the differences 27, 45 and 9. They are all in the table of 9: 27 = 9 × 3, 45 = 9 × 5 and 9 = 9 × 1.
7. The digits 2 and 5 differ by 3, because 5 − 2 = 3. The numbers 25 and 52 differ by 27. These are two different differences.
Answer: 52 − 25 = 27, 72 − 27 = 45, 54 − 45 = 9: the end is 9, and the differences are all in the table of 9

media.teaching_notes: 1. Call the two banks the near bank and the far bank. At the start the lion, the sheep, the grass and the boatman are on the near bank. 2. The boat takes one thing at a time. Only the lion and the grass can be left alone together. 3. Trip 1: take the sheep across. The lion and the grass stay on the near bank, which is safe. The sheep is on the far bank. 4. Trip 2: go back alone. The sheep waits alone on the far bank. 5. Trip 3: take the lion across. The grass is alone on the near bank. The lion and the sheep are on the far bank with the boatman. 6. Trip 4: bring the sheep back. The lion waits alone on the far bank. The sheep and the grass are on the near bank with the boatman. 7. Trip 5: take the grass across. The sheep waits alone on the near bank. The lion and the grass are together on the far bank, which is safe. 8. Trip 6: go back alone. The lion and the grass stay together on the far bank, which is safe. 9. Trip 7: take the sheep across. The lion, the sheep and the grass are all on the far bank. 10. Count the trips: 4 trips to the far bank and 3 trips back, and 4 + 3 = 7 trips. 11. Fewer trips do not work. After the sheep and the lion are both across, going back alone would leave them together, so the sheep must come back once. 12. Check: in every trip the boatman left behind only the lion and the grass, or one thing alone. The sheep was never left with the lion or with the grass. Answer: 7 trips: take the sheep across, go back alone, take the lion across, bring the sheep back, take the grass across, go back alone, take the sheep across

content.text: A boatman wants to cross a river in a boat. He has to take a lion, a sheep, and a bundle of grass with him. He can take one of them at a time. If the sheep and grass are left on the shore, the sheep will eat the grass. And, if the sheep and lion are left on the shore, the lion will eat the sheep. How can the boatman take the lion, sheep, and grass across the river? Help him so that he can ferry the lion, sheep, and grass across the river safely, and in the minimum number of trips.

content.text:
1. Call the two banks the near bank and the far bank. At the start the lion, the sheep, the grass and the boatman are on the near bank.
2. The boat takes one thing at a time. Only the lion and the grass can be left alone together.
3. Trip $1$: take the sheep across. The lion and the grass stay on the near bank, which is safe. The sheep is on the far bank.
[Image: Pastime Mathematics: Ans1: solution]
4. Trip $2$: go back alone. The sheep waits alone on the far bank.
5. Trip $3$: take the lion across. The grass is alone on the near bank. The lion and the sheep are on the far bank with the boatman.
6. Trip $4$: bring the sheep back. The lion waits alone on the far bank. The sheep and the grass are on the near bank with the boatman.
7. Trip $5$: take the grass across. The sheep waits alone on the near bank. The lion and the grass are together on the far bank, which is safe.
8. Trip $6$: go back alone. The lion and the grass stay together on the far bank, which is safe.
9. Trip $7$: take the sheep across. The lion, the sheep and the grass are all on the far bank.
10. Count the trips: $4$ trips to the far bank and $3$ trips back, and $4 + 3 = 7$ trips.
11. Fewer trips do not work. After the sheep and the lion are both across, going back alone would leave them together, so the sheep must come back once.
12. Check: in every trip the boatman left behind only the lion and the grass, or one thing alone. The sheep was never left with the lion or with the grass.
Answer: $7$ trips: take the sheep across, go back alone, take the lion across, bring the sheep back, take the grass across, go back alone, take the sheep across
[Image: Pastime Mathematics: Ans1: solution (continued)]

To find a winning strategy, try playing with $1$ pebble in each pile, two in each, three in each, and so on.

content.text:
1. Let your friend play first. You play second. In one turn a player takes pebbles from one pile.
2. The plan: whatever number of pebbles your friend takes from one pile, take the same number from the other pile.
3. Start with $7$ and $7$. Your friend takes $3$ from the first pile: the piles are $4$ and $7$.
4. You take $3$ from the second pile: the piles are $4$ and $4$.
[Image: Pastime Mathematics: Ans2: solution]
5. Your friend takes $1$ from the second pile: the piles are $4$ and $3$.
6. You take $1$ from the first pile: the piles are $3$ and $3$.
7. Your friend takes $3$ from the first pile: the piles are $0$ and $3$.
8. You take $3$ from the second pile: the piles are $0$ and $0$. You took the last pebble and you win.
9. Why it works: after each of your moves the two piles are equal, such as $4$ and $4$, $3$ and $3$ or $0$ and $0$. Your friend takes from only one pile, so your friend can never empty both piles at once.
10. Check with small piles: with $1$ and $1$, your friend takes $1$ and you take the last one. With $2$ and $2$ and with $3$ and $3$ the same copying wins.
Answer: Let your friend play first. Whatever your friend takes from one pile, take the same number from the other pile. The piles stay equal and you take the last pebble

6. Gap $5$, such as $1$ and $6$: $61 - 16 = 45$, $54 - 45 = 9$. That is $2$ subtractions. Gap $6$, such as $1$ and $7$: $71 - 17 = 54$, $54 - 45 = 9$. That is $2$ subtractions.
7. Gap $7$, such as $1$ and $8$: $81 - 18 = 63$, $63 - 36 = 27$, $72 - 27 = 45$, $54 - 45 = 9$. That is $4$ subtractions.
8. Gap $8$, such as $1$ and $9$: $91 - 19 = 72$, $72 - 27 = 45$, $54 - 45 = 9$. That is $3$ subtractions.
9. $A 1$-digit number comes in the third subtraction for gap $3$ or gap $8$. The pairs are $1$ and $4$, $2$ and $5$, $3$ and $6$, $4$ and $7$, $5$ and $8$, $6$ and $9$, and $1$ and $9$.
10. The numbers they make are $14$ and $41$, $25$ and $52$, $36$ and $63$, $47$ and $74$, $58$ and $85$, $69$ and $96$, and $19$ and $91$.
11. The most subtractions is $5$, for gap $2$. The pairs are $1$ and $3$, $2$ and $4$, $3$ and $5$, $4$ and $6$, $5$ and $7$, $6$ and $8$, $7$ and $9$.
12. Check with $2$ and $4$: $42 - 24 = 18$, $81 - 18 = 63$, $63 - 36 = 27$, $72 - 27 = 45$, $54 - 45 = 9$. That is $5$ subtractions.
Answer: Third subtraction: digits that differ by $3$ or by $8$. Most subtractions, $5$: digits that differ by $2$. The pairs are in the steps

tool_config.idea: Place horse tokens in the square stable and see that counting 5 along each side counts every corner horse twice, so the number of horses is 20 minus the horses in the corner stalls.
tool_config.title: King's Horses Challenge
tool_config.screen: A warm, colourful, polished educational-game scene: the square royal stable of 12 stalls on a soft isometric courtyard with soft shadows and gentle animation, the largest thing on screen. The 4 corner stalls are shaded in a different colour from the 8 edge stalls. Each stall shows its horses as large dots and a number. Controls: tap a stall, then + to add a horse or − to remove one (or drag a horse token from the tray), Check, Undo, Reset, Hint. Read-outs: four side counters, one beside each side (Top, Right, Bottom, Left), each adding the 4 stalls on its side and turning green when it reads 5; a total counter, Horses in the stable, that counts every horse once; a Count one by one button that lights each horse in turn with a running count; and a target card above the stable. A horse placed in a corner stall lights both of its sides. Before the stable, a small practice picture (a practice value, not from the book) shows 12 children in a ring around a square, 4 on each side; tapping a corner child lights its two sides. On every scene: Back and Next in the same place, progress dots and a Restart button.
feedback: A horse placed in a corner stall lights both of its sides and raises both side counters by 1, while the total goes up by 1 only.
A side counter that reads 5 turns green. The total counter shows the real number of horses, each horse counted once.
Count one by one lights each horse in turn, so the student can compare the 4 sides added together with the real number of horses.
A side that does not read 5 shows how many horses it still needs, and Check says which side is short.
tool_config.done_when: Every card is done: the caretaker's stable counted as 19, an arrangement of 18 horses with 5 on each side, and the number of horses the thief can still steal found.

challenges: Corner stall: put one horse in the top left corner stall and nowhere else. Which side counters change, and what does the total show? Answer: the Top and Left counters both show 1, but the total shows only 1 horse.

The caretaker's stable: place the horses as the caretaker did: top row 1, 2, 2, 0; the two middle stalls on the left 1 and 3; the two middle stalls on the right 2 and 3; bottom row 0, 2, 3, 0. Read the four side counters and the total. Answer: every side shows 5 and the total is 19.
Count one by one: press Count one by one on the caretaker's stable. Answer: 1 + 2 + 2 + 0 + 1 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 0 + 2 + 3 + 0 = 19 horses, not 20.
No corner horses: put no horse in any corner stall and make every side show 5. How many horses are there? Answer: 20, because no horse is counted twice.

The 18 horses: The following night, the thief stole another horse from the stable. Now, only 18 horses remained. The caretaker once again cleverly arranged the 18 horses, so that there were 5 horses on each side of the square stable. How do you think he was able to do it? Arrange the 18 horses in the stable with 5 on each side. Answer: 1 horse in the top left and 1 horse in the bottom right corner stall, and 2 horses in each of the 8 middle stalls. Every side shows 5 and 1 + 1 + 8 × 2 = 18. Other arrangements can work too.

How many more: How many more horses can the thief steal before the king notices something is wrong? Try making the arrangements yourself. Answer: the horses = 20 − the horses in the corner stalls. With one horse in each corner stall there are 16 horses, so 2 more after the 18. Taking more means crowding the corner stalls, which the king would notice.

For 18 horses: 20 − 18 = 2, so two horses must stand in corner stalls. Put one in the top left corner and one in the bottom right corner, then fill the other stalls so that every side adds to 5.
The tool places 1 horse in the top left and 1 in the bottom right corner stall and 2 horses in each of the 8 middle stalls. Every side adds to 5 and the total is 18. Then a similar card follows.

media.instructions_for_student: The student sees that counting along the four sides counts each corner horse twice, so the horses in the stable are 4 × 5 minus the horses in the corner stalls.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- King's Horses Challenge
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S30.T30.C126.2D1
- Tool type: Puzzle
- Textbook source: We the Travellers - I, King's Horses: the square stable of 12 stalls, 5 horses counted on each side, the caretaker's arrangement of 19 horses, then 18 horses, and how many more the thief can steal (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that counting along the four sides counts every horse in a corner stall twice, so the horses in the stable are 4 × 5 minus the horses in the corner stalls.
- Out of scope: formulas for other shapes, algebra, dividing the stable into other numbers of sides.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A royal stable courtyard seen from above as a flat illustration: a square ring of 12 pink stalls (4 along the top, 2 down each side, 4 along the bottom) around a white courtyard, on soft green grass. Each stall is about 10% of the stage width. The 4 corner stalls are a deeper pink with a small star. The stable is empty.
- Four side counters sit beside the sides: "Top 0", "Right 0", "Bottom 0", "Left 0". A counter in the courtyard reads "Horses: 0". A round "Count" button sits under it.
- Instruction line: "Put 1 horse in the top left corner stall. Watch the side counters."
- The child is invited to tap the top left stall.
2. Scene and Objects
- A horse is a small flat-drawn horse head in a red circle, like the red dots in the picture. A stall holds up to 5 horses, shown as small circles with a number. Each stall shows a small "+" and "−" when tapped.
- Goal chips: "Corner horse", "4 corner horses", "Sides: 0 of 4", "Count them", "Horses: 0 of 18", "More stolen: 0". In Star Challenge 3 a flat-drawn thief with a sack stands at the top-right of the stage.
3. Main Interaction
- Tap a stall, then "+" to add a horse or "−" to remove one. Tap "Count" and every horse lights in turn with a running count. In Star Challenge 3, drag a horse onto the thief to steal it, and drag horses from stall to stall to rearrange.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" and one big "Check" button that becomes "Next" when the pill is done. "Reset" empties the stable (Star Challenge 1 returns to the caretaker's arrangement).
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Put 1 horse in the top left corner stall. Watch the side counters." Goal chip: "Corner horse". Guess: before adding, the child taps how many side counters will go up: "1", "2" or "4". Result: "Top 1" and "Left 1", the total "Horses: 1". Why: "This horse stands on 2 sides, so 2 side counters count it, but there is only 1 horse." Help: guided, the corner stalls are marked and the two sides light up.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Put 1 horse in each of the 4 corner stalls. What will the four side counters add up to?" Goal chip: "4 corner horses". Guess: the child taps "4", "8" or "16". Result: every side shows 2 and the total shows 4. Why: "2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 counts for 4 horses. Each horse was counted twice, and 8 − 4 = 4." Help: guided, each corner horse lights its two sides.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Make every side show 6 with no horse in a corner stall." Goal chip: "Sides: 0 of 4". Guess: before placing, the child taps how many horses it will take: "20", "24" or "30". Result: each side counter turns green and the total is 24. Why: "No horse is in a corner, so none is counted twice: 4 × 6 = 24 horses." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Make every side show 6 with 1 horse in the top left corner stall and 1 in the bottom right corner stall. How many horses?" Goal chip: "Sides: 0 of 4". Guess: the child taps "22", "24" or "26". Result: every side shows 6 and the total is 22. Why: "4 × 6 = 24 counts, and the 2 corner horses were counted twice: 24 − 2 = 22 horses." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "The king counted 5 horses along each side. We have 5 horses along each side and there are 4 sides. So there are a total of 20 horses, your majesty. But wait, were there really 20 horses in the stable? Count the horses one by one and check! What was the mistake in the caretaker's explanation?" Goal chip: "Count them". The stable shows the caretaker's arrangement: top row 1, 2, 2, 0; left middle stalls 1 and 3; right middle stalls 2 and 3; bottom row 0, 2, 3, 0; every side shows 5. Guess: before pressing Count, the child taps "18", "19" or "20". Then the child presses Count, and then taps the horse that was counted twice. Result: the count ends at 19 and the top left horse glows on 2 sides. Why: "Counting one by one gives 5 + 4 + 5 + 5 = 19. The horse in the top left corner was counted twice: 4 × 5 − 1 = 19." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "The following night, the thief stole another horse from the stable. Now, only 18 horses remained. The caretaker once again cleverly arranged the 18 horses, so that there were 5 horses on each side of the square stable. How do you think he was able to do it? Arrange the 18 horses in the stable with 5 on each side." Goal chip: "Horses: 0 of 18". Guess: before placing, the child taps how many horses stand in corner stalls: "0", "2" or "4". Result: any arrangement with 18 horses and 5 on every side is right, for example 1 horse in the top left and 1 in the bottom right corner stall and 2 horses in each of the 8 middle stalls. Why: "4 × 5 = 20 counts and 20 − 18 = 2, so 2 horses stand in corner stalls: 2 + 8 × 2 = 18." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "How many more horses can the thief steal before the king notices something is wrong? Try making the arrangements yourself." Goal chip: "More stolen: 0". The stable starts with the 18 horses of the example above. Guess: the child taps "1", "2" or "More than 2". The child drags a horse to the thief, rearranges until every side shows 5 again, and presses Check, as often as they like. Result: at 16 horses, with 1 in every corner stall and 3 in the middle stalls of each side, the strip says the sample answer: 2 more. Why: "20 − 4 = 16. With fewer than 16 horses a corner stall holds 2 or more horses, and the king may notice the crowd." Help: independent. Your answer may differ.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Each side counter adds its 4 stalls, so a corner horse is added into two counters. The child compares the side counters with the one-by-one count and sees the extra counts. The rule in the child's words: "A horse in a corner stall is counted on two sides. Horses in the stable = 4 × 5 − the horses in the corner stalls."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the side counters turn green, the horses hop in with a soft chime, the goal chip bounces and the strip says "That is it!"
- Mistake: a side is short -> red strip, small shake, "Left shows 4. It needs 1 more horse." The short side counter pulses.
- Mistake: fixes one side with a corner horse and breaks another -> "A corner horse counts on 2 sides. Check the other side too." Both sides pulse.
- Mistake: says 20 horses in Star Challenge 1 -> "5 + 5 + 5 + 5 counts the corner horse twice. Count each horse once." The top left horse pulses.
- Mistake: wrong total -> "You have 17 horses. The caretaker has 18." The total counter pulses.
- Hints: (1) "How many sides does the stall you are filling touch?" (2) The corner stalls glow and each side counter shows how many horses it still needs. (3) "20 − 18 = 2, so 2 horses stand in corner stalls: put 1 in the top left and 1 in the bottom right."
- Edge cases: a stall holds at most 5 horses, and "−" does nothing in an empty stall. Two horses may stand in one corner stall. In Star Challenge 3 a valid arrangement with fewer than 16 horses is also accepted: "This works too: 15 horses and 5 in the corners. Would the king notice the crowd?"
7. Ending
- Each Activity is done when its goal is met. Star Challenge 1 is done with 19 and the top left horse tapped, Star Challenge 2 with a valid 18, and Star Challenge 3 with any valid arrangement of 16 or fewer horses.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "A horse in a corner stall is counted on two sides." "The horses in the stable are 4 × 5 minus the horses in the corner stalls." "Count the horses one by one to check." Think and talk: "Could the caretaker hide 17 horses so that every side shows 5? How many horses would stand in corner stalls?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: flat courtyard from above with 12 pink stalls and a white middle; red horse-head tokens; deeper pink corner stalls with a star; thief with a sack (flat drawing); four side counters. English only.

content.text:
Once upon a time, there was a king who was very fond of horses. He had 20 horses of the best breed. The horses were kept in the royal stable, and cared for by a caretaker.
One night, a thief stole one of the horses. Fearing punishment, the caretaker arranged the horses in the stable as shown in the picture here.
The next day, when the king came to check on the horses, the caretaker led him around the square stable. "Please count the number of horses along each side, your majesty," he said.
The king counted 5 horses along each side. "We have 5 horses along each side and there are 4 sides. So there are a total of 20 horses, your majesty," the caretaker explained.
Satisfied with the explanation, the king returned to his palace.

content.text:
Worked example: 12 children stand around a square, 4 on each side, with one child at each corner. Sanju adds the four side counts. What does he get, and why is it not 12?
1. Each side has 4 children, counted from corner to corner.
2. Add the four sides: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16.
3. 16 is more than 12, so some children were counted twice.
4. A corner child stands on two sides, so that child is counted once for each side.
5. There are 4 corner children, each counted twice, so there are 4 extra counts.
6. Take the extra counts away: 16 − 4 = 12.
7. Check by counting each child once: 4 corner children, and 2 children between the corners on each side, 4 × 2 = 8. Then 4 + 8 = 12.
Answer: He gets 16, but there are only 12 children, because the 4 corner children are counted twice: 16 − 4 = 12
